I own an enterprise credential-management platform and its privileged access (PAM) product. In practice that means the architecture, the service design, the standards and the roadmap, and just as much the unglamorous work of getting teams to adopt it and being able to show an auditor how it works. Most of my thinking lately goes into a simple question: what happens to identity when the “user” is a service account, a pipeline or an AI agent? That is where this site’s research and writing come from. AI is the future, but humans can’t be replaced. The two work together, with security, governance, monitoring and collaboration.

Started in enterprise technology and ERP delivery, and moved into identity work early. It taught me that access problems are usually process problems. Hands-on with privileged access: onboarding accounts and service accounts into a vault, directory integration, then identity governance, single sign-on and session recording. Risk governance and global delivery, including an on-site assignment in the UK. I learned how the same control reads very differently to an engineer, an auditor and a business owner. Architecture and consulting leadership across India and Australia: PAM strategy, migration plans, onboarding waves, and a current-state assessment and roadmap for a large financial-sector client.

Principal engineering and a PAM Center of Excellence, working across more than one PAM platform. Owning the credential-management platform and the PAM product, with a growing focus on non-human identity and agentic AI.

Make secure access usable, governable and explainable. If people route around a control, the control has failed. Treat identity as the control plane, and start from what the auditor will need to see, not from the tool. Keep things public by design. The case studies here are anonymized and leave out employers, clients and internal data on purpose. Use AI as a co-worker, with privacy, source checks and a human accountable for the result.
If any of these sound like your week, I’m glad to talk. I’m not selling a package here, just starting a conversation.
Planning a move between platforms without losing control coverage, and sequencing onboarding in waves.
Finding and owning service accounts, API keys and AI agent credentials before they become the next incident.
Mapping IAM capabilities to control intent and evidence, so the design holds up when someone asks about it.

Recent credentials include the SailPoint Identity Security Leader credential, CyberArk Certified Delivery Engineer (CPC and PAM), BeyondTrust Password Safe Administrator, CIAM from IMI, and AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate. The full list is on my résumé. I also wrote a 30-page independent study, Securing India’s National Examinations , and publish shorter analysis in Writing .

Structuring research, comparing options side by side and finding gaps in my own reasoning. Tightening writing, especially for executive audiences where every sentence has to earn its place. Analyzing how new things like MCP and AI agents change trust boundaries, permissions and non-human identity. AI is the future, but humans can’t be replaced. The two work together, with security, governance, monitoring and collaboration. Roshan Trivedi

Nothing confidential goes in. No employer, client or internal operational data. That is also why every case study here is anonymized. Sources get checked. If a claim matters, I trace it to something I can link to. A confident answer is not a source. A human stays accountable. AI can draft and challenge. I read it, change it and own what gets published or recommended. AI advises, people decide. The same principle runs through the case studies, from access reviews to break-glass alerts: the model recommends and a person confirms.

The way I use AI is the same way I think agents should be governed: scoped access, clear ownership, evidence of what happened, and a person who can say no. If I can’t apply that to my own workflow, I have no business recommending it to anyone else. Related reading: AI as a Coworker in Identity Operations and Agentic AI Identity Governance .

Owning an enterprise credential-management platform and its PAM product: architecture, standards, service design and the roadmap, with a lot of attention on moving from standing privilege to time-bound access.

Securing India’s National Examinations – A Zero Trust Reference Architecture . A 30-page public-interest proposal applying Zero Trust to prevent exam paper leaks.
A zero-trust reference architecture to prevent paper leaks , protect merit, and rebuild public trust — covering every stage from AI-assisted paper creation to post-exam destruction.

भारत की राष्ट्रीय परीक्षाओं में हर वर्ष 60 लाख से अधिक अभ्यर्थी 5,000 से अधिक केंद्रों पर सम्मिलित होते हैं। प्रश्नपत्र लीक की बार-बार होने वाली घटनाएँ यह दर्शाती हैं कि केवल प्रक्रियागत उपाय परीक्षा की अखंडता की रक्षा नहीं कर सकते। यह प्रस्ताव एक ज़ीरो ट्रस्ट (Zero Trust) सुरक्षा वास्तुकला प्रस्तुत करता है — जिसमें बायोमेट्रिक पहचान, प्रश्नपत्रों का एन्क्रिप्शन, कृत्रिम बुद्धिमत्ता (AI) आधारित निगरानी, तथा सभी केंद्रों की भौतिक सुरक्षा सम्मिलित है। तीन वर्षों की कुल लागत ₹1,419 करोड़ है — प्रति अभ्यर्थी प्रति वर्ष केवल ₹79 — जो एक भी परीक्षा रद्द होने से बचाने पर ही अपनी लागत वसूल कर लेती है।

India operates the world's largest examination infrastructure. A single paper leak cancels an exam for millions and signals that merit doesn't decide outcomes. Examination — Candidates (2024) — Centers — Stakes NEET-UG — 24.06 lakh — ~4,750 — Only gateway to MBBS/BDS in India JEE Main — 11.68 lakh — 500+ — Gateway to IITs, NITs, IIITs CUET-UG — 13.48 lakh — 313 cities — Central university admissions UGC-NET — 9+ lakh — 300+ — Lectureship & PhD eligibility UPSC CSE — ~13 lakh — 72 — IAS, IPS, IFS civil services SSC / Banking / Railways — 5+ crore — Thousands — Government employment
Officials with standing access to papers leak them for financial gain. No SOP prevents a trusted insider from photographing a paper they already hold.
Papers transported without cryptographic protection can be opened and photographed mid-transit with no detection until after the exam.
Systems with weak access controls allow unauthorized bulk downloads of question bank content — often undetected without continuous monitoring.
Proxies sit examinations using forged credentials. Without biometric verification, centers cannot confirm the candidate is who they claim to be.
Without a Security Operations Center, anomalous access at 2 AM before an exam — a classic pre-leak signal — goes completely undetected.
Current security relies on humans following rules under pressure. Architecture-level controls are not optional — they are the only reliable solution.

Four mutually reinforcing pillars, unified by the National Exam-SOC — making a paper leak structurally impossible, not just procedurally prohibited.

Biometric verification, zero standing privileges, and just-in-time access for every person who touches an examination. No account — including administrator accounts — holds permanent access to examination content. All access is JIT, dual-authorised, time-limited, and auto-revoked. PAM platform vaults all privileged credentials. Full session recording. Critical operations require two people to authenticate simultaneously. Re-authentication every 15 minutes.

Papers encrypted from AI-assisted authoring through HSM vaulting to geo-fenced, time-locked decryption at the exam hall. Three simultaneous conditions required for decryption: correct GPS location, authorized time window, two authenticated administrators. Fail any one — paper stays encrypted. Digital watermarking: every copy carries a unique invisible watermark encoding center ID, session, and batch. If a photo leaks online, forensic extraction identifies the source center within minutes.

AI-driven UEBA establishes behavior baselines for every user. Deviations — after-hours access, bulk downloads, unusual location — trigger automated risk scoring. 24×7 National Exam-SOC with SIEM/SOAR. 20 pre-built response playbooks execute automatically in under 2 minutes. Dark web and social media monitoring for paper leaks round the clock.

Every center hardened with certificate-enrolled cameras, metal detectors, signal management, and immutable digital chain of custody. Dedicated encrypted network per center. Local HSM cache device. Computer vision proctoring at Tier A centers. GPS tamper detection on all physical paper packets.

Questions are created through a secure, AI-augmented process with mandatory human oversight at every gate. Paper setters work in physical isolation on air-gapped NTA terminals — no personal devices, no internet, no external communication.

h: Securing the AI That Creates Papers
x: Because AI assists paper creation, proctoring, and anomaly detection, AI itself is an attack surface. Any modern reviewer will ask how it is secured. Here is the answer.
Air-gapped model, sanitized templated prompts, no free-text external input, and output validation prevent the model being steered to leak or bias content.
The syllabus corpus is signed, version-controlled, and integrity-hashed. Every generated question is reviewed by human subject experts.
Liveness detection, multi-modal biometrics (fingerprint + iris + face), and challenge-response defeat synthetic face/voice attacks.
On-premise sovereign hosting, no public API, PAM-gated access, and query-rate monitoring prevent extraction of question patterns.
Mandatory dual-SME approval and a moderation gate mean no unreviewed AI question is ever used in a live paper.
AI assistance can be disabled instantly, reverting to a fully manual, human-only workflow with no loss of security.

Model registry — Every model version registered, signed, and traceable with an approved-use record Model risk assessment — Bias, fairness, robustness, and adversarial testing before deployment Explainability — Proctoring and anomaly models must justify every flag in human-readable terms Sovereign hosting — All models run on Govt of India (MeghRaj / GI Cloud) or NIC — no foreign cloud, no external LLM API Continuous red-teaming — The AI paper tool is adversarially tested each cycle for injection and leakage Audit logging — Every prompt, output, and human decision logged immutably for post-exam audit Aligned to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.

Candidates with identical wrong answers (beyond statistical probability) are flagged. Seat adjacency mapping identifies suspected copying rings.
Unusual registration clusters from a single locality, coaching center, or IP address range are flagged as potential proxy rings.
Social network analysis of registration data identifies clusters linked by phone number, email domain, payment instrument, or device fingerprint — signals of organized fraud.
Candidates completing an exam in statistically abnormal time (too fast, or with suspiciously consistent response cadence) are flagged for review.
Statistically improbable score jumps between attempts, or scores inconsistent with prior academic record, trigger secondary identity verification.
ML models trained on historical leak incidents identify early warning signatures — access pattern changes in the weeks before an exam that preceded past leaks.

Aadhaar — India's national biometric identity system (UIDAI). 12-digit unique identity backed by fingerprint and iris biometrics for ~1.3 billion residents. AES-256-GCM — Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key, Galois/Counter Mode — symmetric encryption providing confidentiality and integrity. CERT-In — Indian Computer Emergency Response Team — national cyber incident response authority under MeitY. CRYSTALS-Kyber — Post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism standardized by NIST (FIPS 203). Quantum-resistant alternative to RSA/ECDH. CRYSTALS-Dilithium — Post-quantum digital signature algorithm standardized by NIST (FIPS 204). Quantum-resistant alternative to RSA/ECDSA. DPDP Act 2023 — Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 — India's primary data protection legislation covering biometrics and personal data processing.

EIN — Examination Identity Number — unique identifier assigned to every person in the examination ecosystem, linked to Aadhaar. Exam-SOC — National Examination Security Operations Center — 24x7 facility monitoring all examination systems. Geo-fencing — A virtual geographic boundary. Decryption of papers is permitted only when the requesting device is within the authorized boundary. HSM — Hardware Security Module — FIPS 140-2 Level 3 device that generates, stores, and manages cryptographic keys in hardware. Keys never exist in plaintext outside the HSM. IGA — Identity Governance & Administration — platform managing the lifecycle of user identities, roles, and access rights.

JIT Access — Just-In-Time Access — access rights granted only at the moment needed, for the minimum duration, automatically revoked thereafter. MEI — Managed Exam Infrastructure — the security baseline all NTA-approved examination centers must meet. NE-PKI — National Examination PKI — dedicated Public Key Infrastructure hierarchy for the examination security program. NIC — National Informatics Centre — Government of India's primary IT infrastructure organization under MeitY. NIST SP 800-207 — NIST Special Publication on Zero Trust Architecture — the definitive guide to ZTA principles and implementation. NTA — National Testing Agency — autonomous examination authority conducting national entrance and recruitment examinations in India.

PAM — Privileged Access Management — security platform governing access by privileged users to sensitive systems and data. SIEM — Security Information & Event Management — platform aggregating and correlating logs to detect threats. SOAR — Security Orchestration, Automation & Response — platform automating security response actions (session suspension, alerting, forensics). UEBA — User and Entity Behavior Analytics — AI/ML technology establishing behavior baselines and alerting on deviations. VSAT — Very Small Aperture Terminal — satellite communications for rural examination centers where broadband is unavailable.

Zero Trust — "Never trust, always verify." All access requests are authenticated and authorized regardless of network location or user seniority. ZSP — Zero Standing Privileges — no account holds permanent access; all privileges are time-limited and automatically revoked.

A quarterly review that asks managers to approve long lists from memory produces a signature, not a control. Dormant access survives every cycle. Give the reviewer evidence on every line: who owns the account, whether it was used, and an advisory keep or revoke suggestion they can overrule. Then let the decision execute from the identity governance system, and check that it worked. A certification is only finished when the access is gone and you can show it. Everything before that is paperwork.

Access certification, or recertification, is the periodic check that the people who hold access should still hold it. On paper it is simple. Every quarter, each manager gets a list of what their people can reach, and ticks keep or revoke. In practice the list is long and the manager does not know what half the entries are. “SG-FIN-RW-04” tells them nothing. They cannot remember whether the person still uses it, so they do the sensible thing under time pressure and approve it all. The campaign closes on schedule, the audit file shows the campaign complete, and the dormant access is still there next quarter.

The review became a rubber stamp instead of a control. The weak point is rarely the tool that sends the emails. It is the quality of what the reviewer sees and what happens after they answer. Four things tend to be missing: Context. Entitlement names that only an administrator can read, with no hint of what they allow. Evidence. No sign of whether the access was ever used, so “keep” is the safe guess. The right reviewer. Managers asked about application roles they have never seen, and nobody asked about the accounts that have no manager at all. Follow-through.
A revoke decision that turns into a ticket, which waits in a queue, and is closed without anyone looking at the target system.

The flow has seven steps, and the same few records travel through all of them. Account and entitlement data comes in from the directory, the applications and the HR feed, and sits next to usage logs. A risk tier decides how often each account is reviewed and by whom. The reviewer sees the line with its evidence and a suggestion. The decision goes back into the identity governance system, which executes it, and a separate check confirms the access is gone. The dots show one review line traveling from source data to a verified revocation. The advisory flag at step 3 helps the reviewer.

It never decides, and the reviewer’s answer is what gets executed. Two choices in this design carry most of the weight. The first is that usage data is joined to entitlement data before the reviewer sees anything, so evidence is part of the question and not a lookup the reviewer has to do. The second is that the identity governance system stays the system of record for the decision and its execution. A revoke does not leave that system as an email asking someone to do something.

“The manager reviews everything” is the default, and it is wrong for a lot of access. A manager knows whether a person still needs access to the team’s shared drive. They usually cannot judge a database role, an admin console permission or a finance approval limit.

What is being reviewed — Who should review — Why Day-to-day access for a person — Line manager — They know the person’s current job and whether it still needs this Application roles with business meaning — Application or data owner — They know what the role allows and who ought to hold it Privileged and admin access — Platform owner, plus the manager’s confirmation of the person — Two questions need two answers: does the person still work here in this role, and does the privilege still match the work Service and machine accounts — The named owner of the system — There is no manager, so the owner is the only person who can say what depends on it Third-party accounts — The internal sponsor of the contract — The vendor will always say keep.

The sponsor answers for the engagement Accounts with no owner — The platform owner, who triages them — Nobody else can. They are reported separately and treated as findings A reviewer should not approve their own access, and should not be the only person who approved it in the first place. The tool can enforce both. Where it cannot, the line is routed to a second reviewer.

This is an illustration, not a specific event. The counts are made up to show the shape of the work.

A manager of eight people gets one spreadsheet with every entitlement, named by technical ID. Nothing shows which lines were used. They approve all of it on the last day, because rejecting something they do not understand feels risky. Revokes, if any, go to a service desk queue by email.

The manager sees plain descriptions, the last-used date and a flag on lines unused for the agreed window. Grouped low-risk lines are confirmed together. The flagged lines get individual attention. An override of a flag needs a sentence, so “keep” on an unused line is a considered choice. Approved revokes execute from the governance system, and the re-read shows them gone.

h: Orphaned, dormant, privileged and service accounts
x: The ordinary employee account is the easy case. The ones that keep surfacing in audits are the accounts the standard flow does not fit. Dormant accounts exist and are valid, but nothing has used them for a long time. A review that shows last use catches them, and a rule that disables them after an agreed period of inactivity catches them between reviews. The review should confirm what the rule has done, not be the only thing that does it. Orphaned accounts have no active owner: the person left, the team was reorganized, the system changed hands.

h: Orphaned, dormant, privileged and service accounts
x: They come out of the inventory step as lines with no person to match. They go to the platform owner, who either assigns an owner within a deadline or disables the account. Privileged accounts get the shortest cycle and a stricter reviewer path. The questions are whether the person still needs this level, and whether the privilege is standing or can be requested when needed. Reviews find the standing access, and the answer is often to move it to request-and-approve rather than keep it. Service accounts have no manager, no leaving date and often no obvious owner.

h: Orphaned, dormant, privileged and service accounts
x: They stay in the same review, with an owner recorded at creation, a purpose, and a note of where the credential is used. The owner is asked to confirm the account still has a job. An account whose owner cannot be found goes onto the orphan list. Movers carry old access into a new role. The review is a backstop. The better control is removing access when the person moves, which is why the HR feed sits at the source end of the diagram.

h: Orphaned, dormant, privileged and service accounts
x: Account type — Review rhythm — What the reviewer sees Standard employee — Set by tier, at least periodic — Description, grant date, last use Privileged — Shortest cycle — Standing or on request, last elevation, last use Service — Set by tier, with owner confirmation — Owner, purpose, where used, last sign-in or token use Third party — Aligned to the contract — Sponsor, end date, last use Orphaned — Triage on discovery — Last known owner, last use, what it can reach

h: Keeping the review from becoming a stamp
x: Evidence helps, but people still find ways to click through. These are the habits I design against. Short packs. A reviewer handed hundreds of lines will approve hundreds of lines. Group the low-risk, recently used access, and spend attention on the rest. Visible agreement. If the reviewer approves a line the system flagged as unused, they give a reason. It takes seconds and it changes behavior. Watch the pattern. A reviewer who approves everything in a few minutes, campaign after campaign, is a finding in itself. Reviewers see their own override and revoke counts, and the platform owner sees the outliers. No silent defaults.

h: Keeping the review from becoming a stamp
x: Unanswered lines escalate and then suspend. Waiting it out is not allowed to be a way to keep access. Spot checks. Security samples a few “keep” decisions each cycle, asks the reviewer why, and checks the answer against the usage record. Respect the reviewer’s time. Review dates are announced early, reminders go out on a schedule, and the pack is ready when the campaign opens. A rushed review is a rubber stamp by design.

An agent is a non-human identity that makes choices at runtime. Give it its own identity, a named human owner, and no standing access. Issue one short-lived credential per task, scoped to one tool, and decide again on every action. Actions that are expensive to undo wait for a person. Record who the agent acted for, not only that it acted. Keep a switch that turns the agent off, and practice using it.

Agent frameworks let an AI pick up scopes, call APIs and launch sub-agents as it goes. The identity a workflow ends up using is decided while it runs, long after anyone provisioned it. Most Identity and Access Management (IAM) stacks assume the opposite: a role is assigned once and holds, and an access review treats a snapshot as a fair description of the account. Neither assumption survives an agent that can ask for a new capability halfway through a job. In practice the first agents in a company tend to arrive through the side door.

Someone creates an API key, pastes it into a framework, and the agent starts working under that person’s authority or a shared service account. Nobody registered it, nobody owns it, and the logs show a human name next to actions that person never saw. I wrote about the sharing side in One Key, Every Agent . I am not arguing for fewer agents. AI is the future of a lot of this work, and humans cannot be replaced in it. The two work best together, with security, governance, monitoring and collaboration around them.
An agent should be easy to adopt and easy to stop, and a person should be able to see what it did and say no when the action is hard to reverse.

Two questions come up in every conversation about agents. Who is the agent, and for whom is it acting? The first is identity and the second is delegation. Keeping them apart makes the design easier. The agent has its own identity. It is a non-human identity, like a service account or a workload, with an entry in a registry. It does not borrow a person’s login or share a key with other agents. The agent has a named owner. One accountable person, with a backup, who can explain what it is for and decides whether it keeps running. A team mailbox does not count.

The agent acts on behalf of someone or something. A user who asked for the task, or a business process that triggered it. That principal is recorded next to every action. Sub-agents get less, never more. If an agent starts another one, the child gets its own identity or a child credential with a narrower scope and a shorter life than the parent’s. OAuth already has the vocabulary for delegation. RFC 8693 (OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange) separates impersonation, where one party becomes indistinguishable from another, from delegation, where the actor keeps its own identity and acts for someone else.

Its act claim names the acting party inside a token, and nested claims can show a chain of actors. For agents I want delegation. A trail that says “this agent, for this user” is far more useful than one that says “the user”. The MCP authorization section I read does not list RFC 8693, so using it in a broker is my suggestion and MCP does not require it.

Agent ID — A stable identity that appears in every token and every log line. Owner, backup and purpose — Someone to ask, and one sentence a reviewer can compare with what the agent really does. Allowed tools and servers — An allowlist. A tool that is not listed is not reachable. Risk tier — Sets how much needs approval and how long tokens may live. Review and expiry dates — A registration that expires unless someone confirms it. Status — Active, suspended or retired. The broker reads this before it issues anything.

The agent asks to act. A policy decision point checks the request against the registry and the rules. A human approves anything above the risk threshold. A credential broker issues a short-lived token for exactly that action. The tool, usually an MCP server, validates the token and acts on the target system. A log records each step, outside the agent’s reach. The dot follows one action. The agent asks, policy decides, a person approves if the action is risky, the broker issues a short-lived token, the agent calls the MCP server, and the server acts on the target system with its own credential.
The numbers match the steps below. Nothing here depends on a specific product; any identity provider, policy engine and gateway that can fill each slot will do.

The steps follow a single action through the diagram. Each has a guardrail, which the design requires, and evidence, which you can show an auditor afterwards. A guardrail with no evidence is a hope. The agent asks to act The agent authenticates as itself and states the task, the tool it wants and the principal it is acting for. With no registry record, or a suspended one, the request ends here. This is the zero standing privilege starting point: the agent holds no access between tasks. Guardrail No registry record or no owner, no access Evidence Registry entry and authentication log

Policy decides, every time The decision point looks at who the agent is, the task, the tool and arguments, the risk tier and what already happened in this task, then decides again on the next action. This is continuous authorization: a new permission request or sub-agent is judged when it appears, and the next review cycle is too late. NIST SP 800-207 has the same idea for zero trust: access per session, with authorization strictly enforced before access is allowed. Guardrail Deny by default, evaluated per action Evidence Decision record with the policy version used

A person approves the risky ones Above the risk threshold the action pauses and goes to an approver, who sees the exact action and its parameters. The approval is bound to that action and expires quickly. This is the pattern from my MCP Human Approval Gateway lab: autonomy stops where a wrong action is expensive to reverse. Guardrail Approval tied to exact parameters, short expiry Evidence Approver, time, parameters shown, outcome

x: The broker issues a short-lived token If the action is allowed, the broker issues a credential for this tool only, with the narrowest scope that does the job and a lifetime measured in minutes. Where delegation matters, the broker mints a token that names both the user and the agent. Guardrail One tool, narrowest scope, short lifetime, audience set to the target server Evidence Issuance log: subject, actor, audience, scope, expiry

h: The broker issues a short-lived token
x: The agent calls the MCP server The server checks that the token was issued for it and that the scope covers this operation. If the scope falls short, it answers with an insufficient scope error, which sends the agent back to step 2. It never widens anything on its own. h: The agent calls the MCP server
x: The server acts with its own credential The server calls the target using its own credential and passes along who the agent is acting for, in whatever form the target accepts. It does not forward the agent’s token. The target still runs its own authorization, so a confused or manipulated agent meets a second check. x: Log, correlate, expire Every step writes to a log that the agent and its owner cannot edit, and a correlation ID ties request, decision, approval, token and call together. When the task ends the token expires. Granted permissions are compared with what the agent really did, so drift shows up as a signal and not as a surprise after an incident. Guardrail Logs held outside the agent’s reach, token expiry as the default stop Evidence One correlated trail per task, plus a permissions-versus-behaviour report

h: Example: an operations agent and a stuck export job
x: This is an illustration, not a specific event. An operations team registers an agent for failed batch jobs. Its owner is the team lead, and it is registered for three tools: read job status, restart a job, and clear temporary files. A user asks it to fix a stalled overnight export. Reading job status is low risk. Policy allows it and the broker issues a read-only token that lives a few minutes. Restarting the named job is medium risk. Policy allows it for that one job, and the token is scoped to that restart. Clearing temporary files is high risk, because deletion cannot be undone.

h: Example: an operations agent and a stuck export job
x: The request pauses, and the approver sees the exact path pattern and how many files it matches. They approve once, for that pattern, and the approval expires. Halfway through, the agent asks for a database administration scope. Policy refuses, because that tool is not on its list. Getting it means the owner changes the registration, and that goes through review.

The agent runs on a personal API key that was pasted into a config file. It can touch everything its creator can touch, all the time. The logs show the creator’s name next to every action. Nobody can say who owns it or when it was last reviewed.

The agent has its own identity and a named owner. Each action gets a short-lived token for one tool. The deletion waited for a person who saw the exact files. The log shows the agent, the user it acted for, the approver and the result.

h: MCP connections and what the specification gives you
x: Many agents reach their tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), so I start with its authorization section. I read the current draft on modelcontextprotocol.io, its security best practices page and the tools page of the 2026-07-28 revision. The specification changes, so check the revision you deploy. These are the points that matter for governance. Authorization is optional, and defined for HTTP transports. Implementations that use stdio should take credentials from the environment instead. A local stdio server therefore sits outside any broker unless you choose to wrap it. My reading is that local servers are a governance gap to plan for.

h: MCP connections and what the specification gives you
x: An MCP server is an OAuth resource server. The client is an OAuth client. The server must publish OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), which tells the client which authorization server to use. Tokens are bound to one server. Clients must send the resource parameter from RFC 8707 (Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0) in both the authorization request and the token request, naming the MCP server the token is for. Servers must validate that a token was issued for them and must not accept or pass on other tokens. Scopes can grow when needed.

h: MCP connections and what the specification gives you
x: A server can answer with a 403 and an insufficient_scope challenge that names what the operation needs, and the client can start a step-up authorization. The security guidance adds that servers should log elevation events with correlation IDs and avoid wildcard scopes. Step-up is the protocol’s version of deciding again at the moment of need, which is where my policy decision plugs in. Token passthrough is forbidden. The security page explains why: it bypasses controls that depend on the token audience, and downstream logs then show a different identity from the one that made the call.

h: MCP connections and what the specification gives you
x: That is an audit argument as much as a security one. A person should be able to say no. The tools page says there should always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations, that clients should prompt for confirmation on sensitive operations and show tool inputs first, that servers must implement access controls and rate limit, and that tool annotations are untrusted unless they come from a trusted server. The authorization section leaves the authorization server implementation out of scope.

h: MCP connections and what the specification gives you
x: It says nothing about who owns an agent, which actions need approval, how to record delegation or how to retire an agent. Those pieces sit around the protocol, and they are what this page is about.

A short token life is the cheapest way to stop an agent, because access ends by itself. It is not enough alone, so I design the stop in layers and test each one. Suspend the agent in the registry. The broker reads the status before issuing anything, so no new tokens come out. Let tokens run out. With lifetimes in minutes, existing access fades quickly. Anything longer-lived, such as a refresh grant, is revoked at the authorization server. Whether an issued access token can be killed early depends on the token type and on whether servers check its status, so I confirm that per system.

Block it at the tool. The MCP server or its gateway keeps a deny list keyed on the agent ID. Rotate what sits downstream. If the agent or its credentials may have been exposed, rotate the secrets the tool uses to reach the target systems. Then the lifecycle, which has three moments. Register. The owner states the purpose, tool list, principals and risk tier. A reviewer approves the registration before the broker issues anything, and it carries an expiry date. Review. On a rhythm tied to the risk tier, the owner confirms the agent is still needed and compares granted permissions with what it did.

Unused permissions are removed. The drift report from step 7 earns its place here. Retire. When the project ends or the agent goes quiet, it is suspended, grants are revoked, downstream credentials are rotated, and the record is kept with its logs. An owner who leaves triggers a reassignment, and with no taker the agent is suspended.

The OWASP guidance on excessive agency is clear that authorization belongs in the downstream system and not in the model’s judgment. Local servers that nobody registered. When an agent runs on a person’s token or a team’s shared key, the logs name the wrong party, the access is wider than the task, and the secret tends to end up in prompts, config files, logs and tool output. The alternative is simple to say. Each agent has its own identity. A broker issues a short-lived credential for one task, scoped to one target, on behalf of a named user. The model never sees the secret. Every record then shows two names: the agent that acted and the person it acted for.
That is what an auditor, and an incident responder, will ask for.

Agents are easy to start and hard to account for. A developer wires one into a ticketing system, a code host, a data store and a cloud account. The fastest way to make that work is to paste in a credential that already works: a personal access token, a team service account, or an API key from a shared vault entry. It works in a demo. It keeps working long after the demo. I see five things go wrong with that shortcut, and they feed each other. Attribution is lost. The target system sees the person’s name, or the team account’s name.

Nothing says an agent acted, which agent it was, or what it was asked to do. If three agents share one key, even the agent’s own team cannot tell them apart. Access is wider than the task. A person’s token carries everything that person can do. An agent that only needed to read tickets can now delete them, read the finance share, or push to production. OWASP lists excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy as the three root causes of what it calls excessive agency. A borrowed human credential supplies the second one for free. Secrets leak into places they should never be.

A key in the system prompt can be repeated back by the model. A key in a config file lands in version control. A key echoed in a tool result lands in the conversation history and the trace store. OWASP’s guidance on system prompt leakage says sensitive data such as credentials and connection strings should not be in the system prompt at all. Tokens live too long. A credential made for a demo is rarely retired. Nobody remembers it exists until it is used by someone who should not have it. One leak means every system.

Because the same key reaches everything the agent touches, a single exposure, whether from prompt injection, a log line or a stolen laptop, is an incident in all of those systems at once. None of this is new. Shared accounts and long-lived keys were a problem long before agents. What agents change is the speed and the number. They make many calls, they chain tools, and they read untrusted text that can steer them. The credential that was risky in a script is riskier when a model decides what to do with it.

h: Why I do not treat this as theory
x: The clearest public example I found is the 2025 compromise of tokens issued to a third-party integration. Between 8 and 18 August 2025, a group tracked by Google Threat Intelligence as UNC6395 used stolen OAuth tokens for the Salesloft Drift integration to pull data out of customers’ Salesforce instances. Google reported being aware of more than 700 potentially affected organizations. By 20 August, Salesloft had started working with Salesforce to revoke all active access and refresh tokens for the Drift application.

h: Why I do not treat this as theory
x: The attackers went through the stolen data looking for secrets such as AWS access keys, passwords and Snowflake access tokens, which is a reminder that credentials pasted into records and notes become a second leak. That incident was about a vendor integration, not an agent run inside someone’s own company. I include it because the shape is the same: a token that was trusted broadly, kept alive, and valid across many customers. Revoking everything was the only fast way to stop it.

h: Why I do not treat this as theory
x: A design where each connection had its own token, scoped and short-lived, would have made the blast radius smaller and the revocation more precise.

h: Two ways to connect the same agent
x: Both designs get an agent talking to the same systems. The top lane is the shortcut. The bottom lane gives the agent a name of its own and puts a broker between the agent and every credential. The broker is a vault or secrets service that can mint or hand out credentials by policy and write the log. In the second design the model decides what it wants to do. It does not hold the key that does it. The warm dots show one shared key reaching everything. The bright dots show a request moving through the broker.

h: Two ways to connect the same agent
x: The numbers match the four moments that matter: the agent asks as itself (1), the broker decides and mints (2), the target checks the token (3), and the log records both names (4). Users and agents are generic labels here, not a particular product. Two details in the lower lane carry most of the weight. The token goes to the tool layer that makes the call. It does not pass through the model’s context. And the target system checks the token on its own.

h: Two ways to connect the same agent
x: OWASP’s guidance on excessive agency says to implement authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on the model to decide whether an action is allowed.

h: Acting for a person without becoming that person
x: The hard part of the better design is how an agent acts on a user’s behalf and still leaves both names in the record. OAuth has a vocabulary for this. RFC 8693, the token exchange specification, separates two ideas. With impersonation, principal A is given all the rights of principal B and is indistinguishable from B in that context. With delegation, A keeps its own identity, and any action is understood to be taken by A representing B. For agents, delegation is the one I want. Impersonation is what a pasted personal token does: the log says Priya did it. Delegation keeps the agent visible.

h: Acting for a person without becoming that person
x: RFC 8693 expresses this with the act claim, which identifies the acting party to whom authority has been delegated, and nested act claims can show a chain of prior actors. A may_act claim states that one party is authorized to become the actor for another. The token request can carry an actor_token that represents the acting party. I do not think every environment needs to implement RFC 8693 literally. Some identity providers offer their own on-behalf-of flows, and some target systems only accept static API keys.

h: Acting for a person without becoming that person
x: The test I apply is the one the RFC describes: after the action, can I see both who acted and who they acted for, and can the agent be switched off without touching the person’s account? The MCP authorization specification adds two useful rules for tool servers. Tokens are bound to their intended audience with the RFC 8707 resource parameter, and a server must accept only tokens issued for it. If it calls an upstream API, it must not pass through the token it received. It uses a separate token issued by the upstream authorization server.

h: Acting for a person without becoming that person
x: The same specification says authorization servers should issue short-lived access tokens to limit the damage of a leak, and that local stdio servers should read credentials from the environment instead of following the HTTP flow. That last point matters: an environment variable is still a secret sitting next to the model’s tools, so I treat it as the weaker option and keep it out of the model’s context.

h: Issuing a credential to an agent, step by step
x: This is the path I would put in front of a team that wants to launch a new agent. Each step has a guardrail that stops a specific mistake and a piece of evidence you can show later. It assumes a person still owns the agent, and that risky actions still go to a person for approval. Agents do a lot of useful work, and the people who own them stay accountable for it. Register the agent as its own identity, with an owner The agent gets a unique identity that is not a person’s account and not a team account.

h: Issuing a credential to an agent, step by step
x: The record names a human owner, a purpose, the environment it runs in and the systems it may reach. Guardrail No owner, no identity Evidence Agent registry entry

h: Register the agent as its own identity, with an owner
x: Write down the tasks and the smallest scope each one needs List what the agent does, such as read tickets, post a comment or close a ticket. Map each task to the narrowest permission on each target. Reading and writing are separate scopes. Destructive actions are separate again. Guardrail Scope decided at design time, per task Evidence Task-to-scope map, reviewed by the system owner

h: Write down the tasks and the smallest scope each one needs
x: Record the delegation when a person starts a task When a user asks the agent to do something, the user’s identity travels with the request. The agent never receives the user’s own credential. It receives a record that says this user asked, for this task, until this time. Guardrail Delegation, not impersonation Evidence Delegation record with user, task and expiry

h: Record the delegation when a person starts a task
x: The agent asks the broker, and the broker decides The agent authenticates to the broker as itself. The broker checks the agent, the user, the task and the target against policy. Actions that change or delete data, or that touch sensitive data, require a person to approve before the broker issues anything. Guardrail Policy check outside the model; human approval for high-impact actions Evidence Decision log and approval record

h: The agent asks the broker, and the broker decides
x: Issue a short-lived, narrow credential and keep it from the model The broker mints or releases a credential for that one task and target, with a lifetime measured in minutes where the target allows it. It is delivered to the tool layer that makes the call. The model gets the result of the call, not the secret. Guardrail Secret never in the prompt, the context or the tool output Evidence Issue record with scope and expiry; prompt and trace scans find no secrets

h: Issue a short-lived, narrow credential and keep it from the model
x: The target authorizes the call and the log keeps both names The target system checks the credential itself and enforces its own permissions. The record carries the agent, the user, the task, the target, the scope and the time. It goes to a log store the agent and its owner cannot edit. Guardrail Authorization in the target system, log kept outside the agent’s reach Evidence Audit record with agent and user identity

h: The target authorizes the call and the log keeps both names
x: Expire, revoke and review The credential ends with the task or at its expiry. If the agent misbehaves, you disable the agent’s identity and everything it can obtain stops with it. The owner re-confirms the agent and its scopes on a regular rhythm, and unused scopes are removed. Guardrail Kill switch on the agent identity; periodic owner attestation Evidence Revocation drill result and attestation record

The agent runs on Priya’s personal access token, which she created last spring. The token can read, edit and delete in the ticketing system and read the customer database. The token sits in the agent’s config file, and the framework prints it in debug traces. Closed tickets show Priya as the actor. Nobody can tell which closures were hers.

The agent has its own identity and a named owner in the support team. For each task it asks the broker for a token that can read tickets, or comment, or close a single ticket. Closing a ticket needs a person to approve it, and the approval is attached to the record. Tokens last minutes and are handed to the tool, never to the model. Closed tickets show the agent as actor and Priya as the person it acted for. An audit record for one action in the second setup might look like this. The values are made up.

Field — Example value — Why it is there Actor — agent: support-summarizer-02 — Which agent acted, down to the instance On behalf of — user: priya — The person who asked, kept from the original request Task and target — close one ticket in the ticketing system — What was done and where Scope — tickets: close, a single ticket — Shows the credential was narrower than the person’s own access Issued and expires — 12:04, expires 12:09 — Shows the credential was short-lived Approval — approval reference from a named person — Links a high-impact action to a human decision

h: How to roll it out without stalling
x: 1. Find where agents already hold credentials Search repositories, pipeline variables, agent configuration and trace stores for keys and tokens. List which agent uses which credential and whose credential it is. Done when There is one list of agents, their credentials and the people behind them. 2. Give each agent an identity and an owner Create an identity per agent and stop issuing new shared keys for agent work. Done when Every active agent has its own identity and a named owner. 3.

h: How to roll it out without stalling
x: Put the broker in front of the first few systems Start with the systems where a leak would hurt most, and those that already support short-lived tokens. Done when Agents reach those systems only through the broker, and the old shared keys are revoked. 4. Carry the user’s identity Add delegation so the record shows the agent and the person it acted for. Add human approval for high-impact actions. Done when An audit record answers who acted and for whom without anyone asking the team. 5. Monitor, drill and retire Alert on an agent touching a system it has never used. Rehearse revoking one agent.

h: How to roll it out without stalling
x: Remove the leftover static keys and the exceptions that have run out of reasons. Done when A revocation drill succeeds on the clock you set, and exceptions have owners and end dates.

Guardrail — What it stops — How you check it One identity per agent, with an owner — Lost attribution and orphaned agents — Report of agents with no owner, or sharing an identity No personal or team credentials in agent configuration — An agent inheriting everything a person can do — Scan agent configuration and pipelines for personal tokens Scope per task and per target — Excessive permissions and wide blast radius — Compare issued scope with the task-to-scope map Short-lived credentials by default — A leaked token staying useful for months — Share of agent credentials with an expiry, and the longest lifetime Secrets kept out of prompts, context and tool output — The model repeating a key, or a trace store holding one — Plant a test secret and search prompts, traces and logs for it Authorization enforced in the target system — Trusting the model to decide what is allowed — Try an out-of-scope call and confirm the target refuses it Human approval for high-impact actions — Excessive autonomy on deletes, payments and bulk changes — Sample high-impact actions and find the approval for each Logs written outside the agent’s reach — Evidence changed by the party it covers — Confirm the agent and its owner cannot edit the log store Tested revocation of an agent identity — Not knowing how to stop a misbehaving agent quickly — Run a drill and time it I keep rotation on this list for credentials that have to be long-lived, such as a static key at a legacy target.

The OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet says to rotate regularly so that stolen credentials work only for a short time. For agents the better lever is to avoid the long-lived credential in the first place, because a credential that expires in minutes needs no rotation schedule.

h: Audit: the questions, and the evidence
x: Question — Where the answer comes from Which agent made this change? — Audit record with the agent’s own identity Which person was it acting for? — Delegation record, carried into the audit record What could the agent reach, and why? — Task-to-scope map and the policy that granted it How long was the credential valid? — Issue record with time of issue and expiry Did a person approve the risky action? — Approval record linked to the action Were any secrets exposed to the model or to logs? — Scan results for prompts, traces and logs, and the exception register Who owns this agent, and when was it last reviewed? — Agent registry and the last attestation Can we turn it off, and how fast? — Latest revocation drill result

I list only what I checked against the published text. Control wording below is paraphrased. AC-6 — Least privilege: allow only the accesses, for users or processes acting on their behalf, that are necessary for assigned tasks. OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 — LLM02 — Sensitive information disclosure, which lists security credentials among the sensitive data, with least privilege as a mitigation. LLM06 — Excessive agency: limit permissions to the minimum, run actions in the context of the specific user, and authorize in downstream systems instead of leaving that to the model.

LLM07 — System prompt leakage: keep credentials and connection strings out of the system prompt, and do not delegate privilege separation or authorization checks to the model. RFC 8693 — Section 1.1, act , may_act , actor_token — Defines delegation and impersonation, and a way to express the acting party in a token. This page does not claim any particular framework certification or regulatory outcome.
It maps a design to the published wording so that a reviewer can check the mapping.

Agent owner — The agent’s purpose, its task list, its scopes and its retirement Credential platform owner — The broker or vault, the issuance policy, rotation and revocation System owners — What each scope on their system means, and the authorization the system enforces Security architecture — Which actions need human approval, token lifetimes and exception criteria Monitoring team — Alerts on unusual agent behavior and the response runbook Internal audit — Independent checking, separate from those who run the controls People stay accountable. I treat an agent as a capable assistant that works under a named owner.

It does not take over the owner’s responsibility. Security, governance, monitoring and collaboration between people and the agent make it safe to rely on. Measure a few things. Share of agents with their own identity, agents without an owner, longest credential lifetime, share of high-impact actions with an approval, and time to revoke one agent. Exceptions have owners and end dates. A legacy target that only takes a static key goes on a register, gets reviewed, and leaves when its reason ends.

The broker becomes the new single point of failure and the new big target. It holds the means to reach many systems. It needs strong access control of its own, high availability, and a plan for when it is down. Agents that cannot reach it will be tempted to fall back to a shared key, so the plan has to cover that case. Scopes are too coarse to be useful. If the target offers only read and write, a read-only task cannot get a read-only credential. I record these gaps and ask the system owner for finer scopes.

Meanwhile a gateway in front of the target can enforce the narrower rule. Delegation turns into impersonation. A flow that quietly passes the user’s own token to the agent looks like delegation in a diagram and behaves like impersonation in the log. I check the log, not the diagram. Secrets still leak through the side doors. Debug traces, error messages, tool output and environment variables are where I find them. Redaction rules catch the formats someone thought of. I prefer designs where the model never receives the secret, and I test with a planted one. Tool servers pass tokens along.

An MCP server or gateway that forwards the token it received to an upstream API recreates the shared key. The specification forbids it, so I check for it. Approval fatigue. If every action asks a person, people click through. Keep approvals for the actions that change or delete data or carry real cost, and make the approval screen show what will happen. Legacy targets resist. Some only accept a static key. Put those behind the broker, keep the key in the vault, restrict who can request it, and track them as named exceptions.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: These are habits I keep when I look at an agent design. They come from how I run credential and access programs. They are not a record of any one project. I ask whose name is on the log before I ask anything else. If the answer is a person who did not do the work, or a team account, the rest of the design review can wait. I look for the secret before I look at the model. I search config, pipelines and traces for keys first. The inventory usually explains the risk better than any architecture slide. I plant a test secret.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: I put a fake key into a prompt, a config and a tool result, then see where it turns up. That finds more than a policy document does. I design for the broker being down. If the only fallback is a shared key, the fallback will become the design. I agree the failure path with the owners before launch. I rehearse the kill switch. I run a drill on one agent and time it. A revocation process that has never been tried is a guess. I keep people in the loop where the damage is hard to undo.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: I am comfortable letting an agent read, summarize and draft on its own. Deleting, paying and bulk changes go to a person. The longer version of how I run a program like this, from the first conversation to the last training session, is in How I Run a Privileged Access Program . t: AI as a Security Product Co-worker
x: AI is the future of this work, and people cannot be replaced in it. The two work together, with security, governance, monitoring and collaboration around them. Treat the assistant like a new team member. It gets a job, a named owner, its own identity, access limited to that job, and a written agreement about what it does alone and what needs a yes. Every connection to a company tool is an access decision. Put a broker and a policy in front of it, keep a human checkpoint on anything that writes, sends or leaves the company, and log all of it.

t: AI as a Security Product Co-worker
x: AI can speed up product and security work. I use OpenAI, ChatGPT and Claude to structure research, compare options and tighten executive writing. The speed is real. So are the risks of ungoverned use: data leaves the building, a confident answer turns out to be wrong, and nobody can say afterwards who decided what. That is the early picture, when an assistant is a browser tab and a person pastes text into it. It changes quickly once the assistant is connected to things.

t: AI as a Security Product Co-worker
x: An assistant that can read the shared drive, query the ticket system and send a message is no longer a tool you consult. It acts, and it acts with some set of permissions. Those permissions belong to somebody. If nobody decided what they should be, they were decided by whoever set up the connection that afternoon. The Model Context Protocol, MCP, makes the connection easy to build. That is useful, and it also means a new kind of non-human identity can appear in a team in a day. The questions I would ask of any new joiner apply here too. What is your job?

t: AI as a Security Product Co-worker
x: Who do you report to? What can you see? What can you change? Who checks your work? Most teams have clear answers for people and no answers for the assistant sitting next to them. This page describes how I would answer those questions. It is a reference approach for a team that wants the speed without giving up accountability.

t: AI as a Security Product Co-worker
h: The idea: a coworker with a job description
x: A coworker has a role. They have a manager, a login, a scope of work and a list of things they should ask about first. When they leave, their access is removed the same week. I apply all of that to an AI assistant, on purpose and in those words, because the habits people already have for new colleagues are good habits. Three questions sit under everything else. What may it read? Which sources, at which classification, for which task. What may it do? Which actions, in which systems, with what limit on size and reach. What may it decide? Almost nothing that matters.

x: Each guardrail is tied to a risk it answers. OWASP names the risk of excessive agency as damaging actions taken in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated model output, and it traces it to too much functionality, too many permissions or too much autonomy. Those three are a useful checklist for any connection I review.

OWASP’s mitigations match what I already do for people: restrict privileges to the minimum, put a human in the loop for privileged operations, and keep untrusted content clearly separated. x: The connection arrives before the agreement. Somebody connects a tool because it takes ten minutes, and the working agreement is written later, if at all. The access then reflects convenience. The assistant borrows a person’s login. Every action looks like the person did it. Logs stop being useful, and the person ends up answering for something they did not do. Checkpoints turn into noise. If every action asks for approval, people click yes without reading. If nothing asks, nothing is checked. The fix is fewer checkpoints on the actions that matter, with enough detail to decide quickly. Reading is treated as harmless.

t: AI as a Security Product Co-worker
x: A read-only connection can still carry a confidential document into a service outside the company, or pull in a page with hidden instructions. Reading needs classification and content handling too. The assistant is never offboarded. The pilot ends, the owner changes team, and the identity and its tokens stay. This is the same orphaned-account problem as with service accounts, and it needs the same ownership discipline. Fear makes people hide it. If the rules are too strict to work with, people use personal accounts and tabs instead, and the company sees none of it. A usable approved path is part of the control.

If a claim matters, I trace it to something I can link to. A confident answer is not a source, and I treat my own use of AI the same way I would ask a team to treat theirs.
