AI collapsed the cost of producing a document, a report or an access request to near zero. It did not collapse the cost of verifying, judging or deciding on that output, and that cost does not disappear. It moves to whoever opens the file next. That cost tends to land on the people with the least slack to absorb it. I call it the processing tax. The fix I specified is structural. A decision-package gate sits where an AI agent hands a request to a human and sends back any handoff that has not done its own thinking first.
It checks completeness, never correctness, so the human keeps the judgment.

This did not start as a thesis. It started as a reaction to a real conversation about AI and workplace productivity, and I wrote it down before I reached for any framework: “AI is creating situations challenging rather than making it easier when it comes to take a decision… it’s not landing properly.” Roshan, reacting in the thread What I was reacting to is a mismatch in costs. Asking an AI tool for a document, a summary, a status report or an access request takes seconds.

Reading that output, checking it, working out what it is really asking for and deciding what to do about it takes about as long as it always did. Sometimes it takes longer, because the output looks finished and the reader has to work out what is missing. Work has two halves: producing the thing and deciding on the thing. Only the first half got cheap. The second half is still done by a person, and a person has a fixed number of hours. When one side of a process speeds up and the other does not, the queue forms in front of the slow side.

The cost also moves in a particular direction. The person who produced the output saved time. The person who receives it pays for that saving. Receivers tend to be the people who decide: approvers, managers, reviewers, owners. These are the people with the least room in their day, because deciding is their job on top of everything else. So the cost concentrates upward, toward the people least able to absorb it. In identity and access work this is easy to picture. An AI agent can raise a hundred access requests before lunch. Each one is cheap to send.

Each one asks a human for a yes or a no. If the request arrives as a bare ask with no analysis attached, the approver has to rebuild the thinking from scratch every time, and approval becomes a chore the approver learns to get through quickly.

h: What the research says, and what it does not
x: I did not want to build a control on one conversation, so I checked the reaction against four independent sources. They measure different things, and none of them measures the processing tax directly. What they have in common is that the gains people expect from AI are harder to find than the speed of producing output would suggest. BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab coined the word “workslop” in a Harvard Business Review article in September 2025. BetterUp’s own write-up defines it as AI-generated content that looks polished and complete but is unhelpful, low-quality or off the mark.

h: What the research says, and what it does not
x: The article’s point that matters here is where the effort goes: onto the colleagues who have to revise or replace it. MIT Media Lab’s Project NANDA published “The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025” in July 2025. It looks at why enterprise AI projects stall, and a core reason it gives is that most systems do not retain feedback, adapt to context or improve over time. I read this through a trade-press summary, not the report itself. NBER executive surveys.

h: What the research says, and what it does not
x: Two NBER working papers survey senior executives about AI and productivity, one of nearly 6,000 executives across four countries and one of about 750 corporate executives. The second reports a disconnect between the productivity gains executives perceive and the gains that are measured. Goldman Sachs Research , in March 2026, said it still found no meaningful relationship between productivity and AI adoption at the economy-wide level, while finding gains in specific use cases such as customer support and software development. I read this through a news report on the note, not the note itself. I would not stretch these into proof.

h: What the research says, and what it does not
x: Some are surveys of opinion, some are trade-press summaries of a report, and none looks at approval queues. My claim is narrower. Four unrelated measurements point the same way: producing output got cheap, and turning that output into a result did not.

h: Why a human reviewer is not enough on their own
x: Putting a person at the end of the line does not fix the problem, because people who check automated recommendations can drift into agreeing with them. Researchers call this automation bias. In a well-known 1999 study of a simulated flight task, Skitka and colleagues found that people using a slightly unreliable automated aid made two kinds of error: they missed events the system did not flag, and they followed its recommendations even when other valid indicators contradicted them. A 2012 systematic review by Goddard, Roudsari and Wyatt looked at how often this happens, what influences it and what reduces it. Regulators have noticed too.

h: Why a human reviewer is not enough on their own
x: Article 14 of the EU AI Act, on human oversight of high-risk AI systems, says the people assigned to oversight should remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output of the system. I read this as support for a design point. If a human is the safeguard, the way the work reaches them decides how well they can do it. A bare yes-or-no ask invites a quick yes. A package that sets out options, a recommendation and a confidence level gives the person something to disagree with.

The diagram shows the same handoff two ways. In the top lane, an AI agent sends a raw request straight to a human approver, who has to verify it, rebuild the context and decide. All the effort lands on one person. In the bottom lane, the agent first builds a decision package. A gate checks that the package is complete. A complete package reaches the human as a quick judgment call, and an incomplete one goes back to the agent with the gap named. The cyan dots are requests moving along each path. The amber dot is an incomplete package going back to the agent.

HumanGate is the name of my own project where the gate lives. The same shape works for any agent-to-human handoff. The gate checks completeness, not correctness. It cannot tell whether the agent’s recommendation is right. It can tell whether the agent did its own thinking, and that is the part a rule can check reliably. The right-or-wrong call stays with the human. Status: this gate is live in HumanGate. The scenario where an AI hands off without doing its own analysis now gets rejected before a human ever sees it.

Steps 3 and 4 are the control itself. Before a request reaches a human, the originating agent must supply the options it considered, its recommendation, a confidence level and the one question that needs human judgment. The other steps are how I would wire that control into a working process. Each step has a guardrail and the evidence it leaves behind. Decide that a human is needed The agent only hands off the decisions that policy says need a person. Everything else it handles inside its own limits.
A handoff is a cost, so the list of things that qualify should be short and written down. Guardrail A catalog of decisions that need a human Evidence Reason code on every handoff

h: Decide that a human is needed
x: Do the analysis first The agent works out what it is asking before it asks. It lists the options it considered, including the option of doing nothing, and picks one. This is the work the approver would otherwise do. Guardrail No handoff without a recommendation Evidence Options considered, as recorded

Build the decision package Four required fields: the options considered, the recommendation, a confidence level, and the one question that actually needs human judgment. The last field forces the agent to narrow a broad ask down to the part only a person can answer. Guardrail Fixed package format with required fields Evidence The package as submitted

Check it for completeness The gate looks for the required fields. It does not judge whether the recommendation is good. A package missing a field goes back to the originating agent automatically, with the specific gap named, before a human sees it. Guardrail Incomplete package is rejected, not queued Evidence Rejection record with the missing field

Put it in front of a person with a clock The approver sees the package, the risk score and a live countdown to expiry. The approval is time-boxed, so a stale request lapses instead of waiting to be approved by habit. The gate sits next to these existing controls as a fourth check: has this request earned a human’s attention. Guardrail Time-boxed approval with risk scoring Evidence Approval timestamps and the risk score shown

h: Put it in front of a person with a clock
x: Let the human disagree, and say why The person can accept, change or refuse the recommendation. A refusal costs them nothing and needs only a short reason. If saying no is harder than saying yes, the package turns into a rubber stamp. Guardrail Reject and modify are first-class options Evidence Decision and reason, recorded

h: Let the human disagree, and say why
x: Check the recommendations afterwards Because the gate only checks completeness, correctness has to be checked somewhere else. A periodic look at a sample of past packages, comparing what the agent recommended with what the human decided and what happened next, shows whether the recommendations deserve the trust they get. Guardrail Regular sampled review of past handoffs Evidence Review notes and agreement rate with human decisions

This is an illustration of the idea, not a description of a real event or a real system. Say an AI agent that supports a delivery pipeline needs write access to a data store so a release can finish. It has to ask a person.

The approver receives one line: please approve write access for the pipeline account. They have to find out which store, why, for how long and what the alternatives are. They either spend a chunk of their day investigating or they approve to clear the queue. Nobody can later see what was weighed.

Options: read-only access, time-boxed write access, or decline and finish the release by hand. Recommendation: time-boxed write access, ending when the release does. Confidence: medium, because the agent could not confirm which tables the release touches. The one question: is the release window a good enough reason to allow write access outside the usual process? In the second case the approver reads a short package and answers a single question. They can still say no, and they can still notice that the confidence is only medium and ask for the table list first.
If the agent had left out the confidence level, the gate would have sent the request back before the approver saw it.

h: How to build it without stalling
x: 1. Map the handoffs List where AI agents and tools pass work to people today: access requests, approvals, reviews, exceptions. Note who receives each one. Done when Every handoff has a named receiver and a rough sense of how often it happens. 2. Define the package Agree the required fields with the people who receive the requests. Ask them what they wish every request already contained. Done when A receiver can read a sample package and say it answers their usual questions. 3. Run the gate in watch mode Check packages and report what would have been rejected, without blocking anything yet.

h: How to build it without stalling
x: Done when The reasons for rejection are understood and the agents can fix them. 4. Turn on enforcement Start with the handoffs that reach the busiest approvers and the highest-risk decisions. Done when An incomplete handoff cannot reach a human in the covered flows. 5. Review and tune Sample past packages, collect feedback from approvers, and adjust the fields and the list of decisions that need a human. Done when The review runs on a fixed rhythm and someone owns the changes that come out of it.

Guardrail — What it stops — How you check it Required decision-package fields — Bare requests that push all the thinking onto the approver — Submit a package with one field missing and confirm it is rejected Automatic return with the gap named — Incomplete requests sitting in a human queue — Rejection record shows the specific missing field and the time A short list of decisions that need a human — Agents asking people about everything — Compare handoff reason codes with the written list Time-boxed approvals with a live countdown — Stale requests approved out of habit — Confirm an expired request cannot be approved Risk score shown beside the package — A low-risk and a high-risk ask looking identical — Review a sample of scores against the decisions they covered Refusal is as easy as approval — Rubber-stamping — Check the interface; look at how often people refuse or change a recommendation Sampled review of past packages — Trusting a recommendation source nobody checks — Review notes on a fixed rhythm, with an owner A caution on the gate itself.

A package can be complete and still wrong, and a confident, well-formatted wrong answer is more persuasive than a messy one. The gate keeps the work off the approver. It does not replace the approver’s judgment.

h: Audit: the questions, and the evidence
x: Question — Where the answer comes from Why was a human asked about this? — The reason code on the handoff and the catalog of decisions that need a person What did the agent recommend, and what else did it consider? — The decision package as submitted Was every handoff complete before a person saw it? — Gate records, including rejections and the gaps they named Who decided, when, and why? — Decision record with the person, timestamp and reason Did the person agree or disagree with the agent? — Decision compared with the recommendation in the package Are the agent’s recommendations reviewed afterwards? — Sampled review notes and who owns them

Standard — Reference — What it asks for NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1) — GOVERN 3.2 — Policies and procedures that define roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems. MAP 3.5 — Processes for human oversight are defined, assessed and documented in accordance with organizational policies. EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 — Art. 14(1) — High-risk AI systems are designed so that people can effectively oversee them while in use, with appropriate human-machine interface tools. Art.

14(4)(b) — The people given oversight remain aware of the possible tendency to automatically rely, or over-rely, on the output of the system (automation bias). Article 14 applies to high-risk AI systems as the Act defines them. Whether a given internal agent is in that category is a legal question, and I do not answer it here. The reference is useful either way because it names the risk the gate is designed around.

Control owner — The gate, the required fields and the list of decisions that need a human Agent owners — The quality of what their agents hand over, and fixing rejections Approvers — The decision itself, including the right to refuse and to ask for more Security architecture — Risk scoring rules and which decisions are high risk Internal audit — Independent checking, separate from those who run the control A rule that is enforced beats a culture that is hoped for. A norm such as “think before you send” only works while everyone remembers it.

The gate holds the line in the exact place the handoff happens. Ask the receivers. The people who approve are the ones who know what a good package looks like. They should help set the required fields and review them on a rhythm. Watch the receiver’s load. Useful signals: how many handoffs reach each approver, how many are rejected at the gate, how often approvers refuse or change a recommendation, and how often a request expires unanswered. Pick the measures, then look at the trend, not a single day. AI advises, people decide. The gate exists to protect that sentence in practice.
The agent recommends and a person confirms, with the evidence in front of them.

Agents learn to fill the fields. A complete package can be padded to pass the check. Options that are not real options, confidence that is always high. Sampled review is the answer to that, and it needs a human to read the packages. The package becomes more reading. If the required fields are long, the gate has moved the tax and not reduced it. Keep the package short enough that a busy approver reads all of it. Over-reliance continues. A well-made package makes agreement easy.

The research on automation bias suggests this is a risk, so the refusal path, the time-box and the sampled review all matter. The list of human decisions grows. Every team has a reason to add one more. Without an owner trimming the list, the number of handoffs creeps back up. Rejections frustrate the agent owners. Early on, many packages will bounce. Watch mode before enforcement gives owners time to fix the common gaps. Review fatigue is real in practice and hard to measure. I have not found a source on it that I could verify, so I do not cite one.
I treat it as something to watch in the load measures above.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: These are habits I keep, not a checklist from any one project. Start from a real reaction. I begin with something someone said or something I felt when I used a tool, then check it against evidence. If I cannot find evidence, I say so and keep the idea small. Separate what I have read from what I have measured. A survey of executives and a measured outcome are different things. I say which one I am quoting, and I say when I read a summary and not the original. Ask who pays.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: When someone says a tool saves time, I ask who gets the time and who gets the extra work. The answer often shows up two steps later in the process. Prefer a control to a reminder. If I want a behavior, I try to build the check into the place where it happens. A reminder fades. Check completeness in the system, and judgment with people. I let the machine do what a rule can verify and keep the call with a person who can say no. Make saying no cheap. If refusing needs a long explanation, people stop refusing.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: I look at that first when a review process starts to feel like a formality. Review the recommender, not just the decision. A good decision process includes a look back at whether the advice was any good. My broader view of how AI and people should work together is on How I Use AI, and where I stop . The same principle runs through the other case studies: the model recommends and a person confirms.

Audit wording and platform settings describe the same risk in different languages. The gap between them is where evidence goes missing and ownership gets vague. Close it with a control register: one row per control, with a plain objective, one owner, the system setting that enforces it, the evidence it produces, and how fresh that evidence must be. Collect evidence by a scheduled job into a store the audited people cannot edit. Record every gap with an owner and an expiry date. Then one control can answer to several frameworks without being written twice.

An auditor reads a requirement such as “access is reviewed periodically”. An engineer reads a screen of group settings. A control owner reads a policy paragraph. All three are talking about the same risk, and each of them is sure the other two have the proof. The trouble shows up when the question arrives. Someone asks to see the last review of privileged access, and the answer is a search through email, a screenshot taken for a different purpose, and a person who has since moved teams. The control may well have been working.

Nobody can show it, and the weeks spent reconstructing proof are weeks not spent improving anything. The work I contributed to was evaluating IAM control intent against what the platforms could actually do and what the operating process actually did. The aim was a plain path from each design decision to the evidence that shows the control works, with a named owner at each point and a review that someone really performs.

Every control gets the same chain. The objective says what the rule is for. The control says what the organization does about it. The system configuration is where that action is switched on. The configuration produces records, and a job gathers those records into a store. The auditor’s question is answered from that store, and what the auditor finds feeds back into the control. The register sits across the top and holds the owners, the frequency and any exceptions.

The dots follow one control through the chain, from its objective to the question an auditor will ask, and back to the control when a finding changes it. The bars show what sits alongside: the register that owns each row, and an evidence store that control owners and platform admins can read but not edit. The register is the part people skip, so it is worth saying what a row holds. Control ID and objective. One sentence in plain words, written so a non-specialist could check it. Control statement. What is done, by whom, how often. Control owner.

One named role accountable for the control working. System and configuration. The setting, policy or workflow where the control lives. Evidence type, source and owner. What proves it, where it comes from, and who collects it. Freshness. How recent the evidence has to be to count. Framework tags. The requirements this one control is read against. Gaps and exceptions. Each with an owner, a reason, a compensating step and an expiry date.

h: Four kinds of evidence, and what each one cannot show
x: Auditors collect evidence by examining records, interviewing people and testing the system. NIST’s assessment guidance names those three methods. An interview helps explain a control, but it is the weakest thing to rely on, so I design for the first and third. That means records the system produced and results anyone can re-run. Evidence type — What it shows — Where it is weak — Freshness it needs Configuration export — How a setting stands at one moment, such as a policy, a group list or a rotation rule — Says nothing about the weeks before or after.

h: Four kinds of evidence, and what each one cannot show
x: A change last month is invisible. — Taken on the collection date, and again after every change to that setting Log query — What happened across a period: sign-ins, approvals, privileged sessions, changes — A wrong query or a missing log source looks the same as a clean result — Covers the whole audit period. The query text is saved with the result. Ticket or approval record — A person asked, another person approved, the work was done — Proves the process ran for that item, not that every item went through it — Per item.

h: Four kinds of evidence, and what each one cannot show
x: Pair it with a list of all changes so the tickets can be matched to the whole population. Review record — A named person looked at a list and decided to keep or remove each entry — Rubber-stamping. A signature without the list and the decisions proves very little. — Dated inside the review cycle, with the list as it stood on the day Most controls need two types together. A configuration export shows the rule. A log query or review record shows the rule was followed over time.

Evidence goes stale. A screenshot from last year proves what a setting looked like last year. Each register row carries a freshness rule, and the collection job is built around it. Frequency also has to follow the strictest framework the control answers to. CIS Controls v8, for example, asks that active accounts are validated as authorized at a minimum of quarterly, and PCI DSS v4.0 asks for user accounts and privileges to be reviewed at least once every six months. A quarterly review satisfies both. Sampling is the auditor’s call, and how many items they pick is theirs to decide.

What I can control is the population they pick from and how the picks are recorded. The population is complete. A full export of accounts, tickets or changes for the period, with the date and query that produced it. A sample from an incomplete list proves nothing about the rest. The pick is recorded. How items were chosen, by whom, and when. If the auditor chooses, their selection is saved as it was given.

h: Mapping one control, step by step
x: Write the objective in plain words Take the requirement as the framework words it, then restate it as one sentence about the risk. If the owner cannot read the sentence and say whether it is true, rewrite it. Guardrail No jargon the owner cannot check Evidence Register row

h: Write the objective in plain words
x: Write the control and name one owner State what is done, by whom and how often. One role is accountable. A committee is not an owner, and neither is a team mailbox. Guardrail A row with no named owner does not go live Evidence Owner field and approval of the row

h: Write the control and name one owner
x: Point to the configuration Name the system and the exact setting, policy or workflow that makes the control real. If the control depends on a person remembering, mark it as a manual control and plan its evidence accordingly. Guardrail Manual controls are labeled as manual Evidence Configuration export

Choose the evidence and its freshness Pick the evidence type from the four above, name the system it comes from, and set how recent it must be. Name a second evidence type if one alone would leave a gap, as with a setting that is shown but not shown to have been followed. Guardrail Every row names its source and freshness Evidence Evidence plan in the register

h: Choose the evidence and its freshness
x: Collect by job, into a store people cannot edit A scheduled job pulls the evidence and writes it to the store with the date, the source and the query. Control owners and platform admins can read it. They cannot change it. Guardrail Collection is automated and the store is read-only to the audited Evidence Collection log and store permissions

h: Collect by job, into a store people cannot edit
x: Review it, and sign the review A reviewer who is not the collector looks at what arrived. They check that it is complete, current and answers the objective. Their name and the date go on the record. Guardrail The reviewer is not the person who collected Evidence Signed review record

h: Review it, and sign the review
x: Record gaps and exceptions with an expiry Where the control or its evidence falls short, write it down. Each entry gets an owner, a reason, a compensating step and an end date, and it comes back to the reviewer on that date. Guardrail No exception without an expiry Evidence Exception register

h: Record gaps and exceptions with an expiry
x: Rehearse the auditor’s question Ask the question the way an auditor would and answer it from the store alone, with nobody going to find a screenshot. Fix what breaks, then update the row. Guardrail Dry run before the audit, and after a major change Evidence Dry-run notes

This is an illustration of one row, not a record of a real control or a real audit. It shows how one control carries its own evidence through the chain. Part of the row — What it says (illustrative) Objective — People who hold privileged access still need it. Access that is no longer needed gets removed. Control — Every quarter, the owner of each privileged group reviews its members and confirms or removes each one. Removals follow within the time the standard sets. System configuration — Privileged groups are listed in the directory, each tagged with an owner.

The review workflow pulls membership for those groups and no others. Evidence source — Membership export when the review opens, the review record with a decision per member, the removal tickets, and a membership export after the removals. Evidence collection — A scheduled job writes both exports to the evidence store with date and query. The review record is exported when the review closes. Freshness — A review record dated within the last quarter. Exports from both ends of the review. Owners — Control owner: head of the team that runs access reviews. Evidence owner: the person who runs the collection job.

Reviewer: someone from risk or security who is neither of those. Exception — A group whose owner has left. Recorded with an interim owner, the reason, and an end date by which a new owner must be named. Auditor’s question — “Show me the last review of this admin group, and who was removed.” Frameworks — AC-2 and AC-6(7) , PR.AA-05 , A.5.18 and A.8.2 , CIS 5.1 , PCI DSS 7.2.4 , SOC 2 CC6.3 The answer to the auditor comes out of the store in minutes: both exports, the decisions, the tickets, and the reviewer’s sign-off.

Frameworks overlap heavily on IAM. Account review, least privilege, authentication and logging turn up in all of them. Writing a separate control for each framework produces duplicates that drift apart, so I write the control once and tag it. Map many to one, and read the words. The review control above carries six tags. They are not word-for-word equal. Some cover all user accounts, some only privileged ones, some only service accounts. Where scope differs, the control statement widens until it covers the largest scope, or a second row covers the remainder. Treat the mapping as my reading.

A framework does not say a particular control meets it. The auditor and the framework owner decide that. The tag records who mapped it, when, and on which version of the standard. Keep the register framework-neutral. Frameworks change versions. A register organized by control survives a new standard. One organized by a standard does not. The full list of references I checked is in the standards map further down.

If the people running a control also control its evidence, the evidence is only as good as their honesty on the worst day. The people involved can be entirely trustworthy and the arrangement is still weak, because the auditor cannot tell the difference. NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 covers this under AU-9, protection of audit information. The base control is to protect audit information and audit logging tools from unauthorized access, modification and deletion, and to alert when it happens. Its enhancements describe the means.

They include storing audit records on a physically different system from the one audited ( AU-9(2) ), limiting who can manage audit logging ( AU-9(4) ), dual authorization for moving or deleting audit information ( AU-9(5) ) and read-only access ( AU-9(6) ). PCI DSS v4.0 has the same intent in requirement 10.3.2, which asks that audit log files are protected to prevent modifications by individuals. Separate the store from the system. Evidence for a platform lives somewhere the platform’s admins cannot write. Write once, read many. Control owners and admins read.

A small, named group holds the right to manage the store itself, and its changes are logged. Prove the lock. Try to edit an item with an owner account and an admin account, and keep the failed attempt as evidence.

h: Gaps and exceptions, with an end date
x: Some controls will not work as written, and some evidence will not exist. A register that shows everything green is either wrong or hiding things. A good one shows a few honest gaps, each with a plan. A gap is a control or its evidence falling short of what the register says it should be. It is recorded the day it is found. An exception is a decision to accept the shortfall for a while. It needs an owner who accepts the risk, a reason, a compensating step, and an expiry date. Expiry forces a decision.

h: Gaps and exceptions, with an end date
x: On the date, the exception is closed because it is fixed, renewed by the same approver with a fresh reason, or escalated. Letting it run on silently is the one thing it cannot do.

h: Preparing for internal and external audit
x: Internal and external audits ask for similar things in different tones. Internal audit usually wants to find problems early and will accept a recorded gap with a plan. External audit wants the control demonstrated across the period and has less room for surprises. The same register and store serve both. Walk the scope with the auditor first. Which controls, which period, which systems. Agree it in writing so the register and the request list line up. Run the register against the request list. Every item the auditor asks for should map to a row.

h: Preparing for internal and external audit
x: Items that do not map point to a missing control or a missing row. Hand over by link and permission, not by email. Give the auditor read access to the relevant part of the store. Everything they pull is logged, and there is one copy of each item. Treat findings as register changes. A finding becomes an update to the control, the configuration or the evidence plan, with an owner and a date, and goes back through the chain.

h: How to build it without stalling
x: 1. Start the register small Pick the IAM controls that matter most and write one row each, in plain words, with an owner. Done when Every row has an objective, a control statement and a named owner. 2. Map to systems and evidence For each row, find the real configuration and the real evidence source. Mark the gaps honestly. Done when Every row points to a setting and a source, and every gap has an entry. 3. Automate collection and lock the store Replace hand-gathered screenshots with scheduled exports and saved queries. Done when The highest-risk controls collect their own evidence into a read-only store.

h: How to build it without stalling
x: 4. Rehearse Answer real auditor questions from the store, with someone outside the team asking. Done when The questions get answered without anyone going to find a file. 5. Keep it alive Review the register on a rhythm and whenever a system, a framework version or an owner changes. Done when The register changes in the same week as the system it describes.

Guardrail — What it stops — How you check it One named owner per control and per evidence item — Controls everyone assumes someone else covers — Report of rows with an empty or departed owner Evidence collected by job — Proof assembled the week before the audit — Compare collection timestamps with the schedule Evidence store read-only to the audited — Edits by the people the evidence describes — Try an edit as an owner and as an admin, and keep the result Query text and run details saved with each result — Results nobody can reproduce — Re-run an old query and compare it with the stored result Exceptions carry an owner, a reason and an expiry date — Temporary gaps that become permanent — List of exceptions past expiry Reviewer is not the collector — Self-marked homework — Compare the two names on each record Register reviewed when systems or standards change — A register that drifts from reality — Date of last review on each row Dry run before every audit — Surprises in the audit room — Pick a control at random and answer from the store alone

h: Audit: the questions, and the evidence
x: Question — Where the answer comes from Which controls cover this requirement? — The register, filtered by framework tag Who owns this control, and who supplies its evidence? — The owner and evidence owner fields Show me it working across the whole period. — Saved log queries and review records for each cycle in the period How do you know this evidence was not changed? — Store permissions, the access list, and the record of the edit attempt What was not working, and what did you do? — Gap and exception register, with owners and expiry dates How was this sample picked? — Sampling record with the full population export and the method Who checks the people who collect? — Reviewer sign-off on each record, and the internal audit report Questions specific to privileged access and credentials are in the audit sections of PAM Modernization & Zero Standing Privilege and Credential Management Platform Strategy .

Standard — Reference — What it asks for NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — AC-2 , AC-6(7) — Review accounts for compliance with account management requirements at a defined frequency, and review privilege assignments periodically. IA-2 , IA-5 — Uniquely identify and authenticate users, and manage authenticators across their lifecycle. AU-2 , AU-12 — Decide which events are logged, and generate the audit records for them. AU-6 — Review and analyze audit records at a defined frequency, and report findings to defined roles. AU-9 — Protect audit information and logging tools from unauthorized access, modification and deletion.

CA-7 — A continuous monitoring strategy with metrics, frequencies for monitoring and for assessing control effectiveness, analysis, response and reporting. NIST CSF 2.0 — PR.AA-01 , PR.AA-05 — Identities and credentials are managed. Permissions are defined in policy, managed, enforced and reviewed, with least privilege and separation of duties. GV.RR-02 , GV.OV-03 , ID.IM-01 — Roles and responsibilities are established and enforced. Risk management performance is evaluated. Improvements are identified from evaluations.

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (secondary summaries) — 9.1 — Decide what to monitor and measure, the methods, who does it and when, when results are analyzed and by whom, and keep documented information as evidence of the results. A.5.15 , A.5.16 , A.5.17 , A.5.18 , A.8.2 — Access control, identity management, authentication information, access rights and privileged access rights. A.8.15 , A.5.35 , A.5.36 — Logging, independent review of information security, and compliance with policies, rules and standards.

CIS Controls v8 — 5.1 , 5.3 , 5.5 — Inventory accounts and validate them at least quarterly, disable dormant accounts after 45 days where supported, and review service accounts at least quarterly. 6.1 , 6.2 — A documented process for granting access and for revoking it. 8.2 , 8.9 , 8.11 — Collect audit logs, centralize them, and review them to detect anomalies. PCI DSS v4.0 (read via secondary) — 7.2.4 , 7.2.5.1 — Review user accounts and privileges at least every six months. Review application and system account access at a frequency set by targeted risk analysis.

10.2.1.2 , 10.3.2 , 10.5.1 — Log all administrative actions, protect audit logs from modification by individuals, and retain history for at least 12 months with the latest three months immediately available. SOC 2 (AICPA TSC) — CC4.1 , CC6.2 , CC6.3 , CC7.2 — Ongoing or separate evaluations of controls. Registering and authorizing users before access. Authorizing, modifying and removing access by role with least privilege and segregation of duties. Monitoring for anomalies.

Control owner — That the control is designed well and works. Answers for gaps and signs exceptions for their area. Evidence owner — That the evidence is collected on time, complete and saved with its source and query. Keeps the collection job running. Reviewer — An independent check that the evidence is complete, current and answers the objective. Not the control owner and not the collector. Register keeper — The structure of the register, framework tags and the review rhythm. Does not own the controls themselves.

Internal audit — Independent testing of the whole arrangement, separate from those who run the controls and those who review them. Separate the three jobs. The person who runs a control, the person who collects its evidence and the person who reviews it should not all be the same person. Where a small team makes that impossible, record the overlap as an exception with a compensating check. Review on a rhythm. The register gets a regular review, and an extra one when a system, an owner or a framework version changes.

The register becomes a spreadsheet nobody opens. If updating it is separate work from changing a system, it will fall behind. Tie the register change to the system change. Evidence is built for the audit. A burst of screenshots the week before only proves the week before. Collection by job fixes this. Everything gets mapped to everything. Tagging a control to a requirement it only loosely touches makes the mapping look complete and wastes the auditor’s time. Tag only what the control really answers. Review turns into signing. If the reviewer sees only a form and never the list, the review proves nothing.
The record must hold the list as it stood and the decision for each item. Exceptions pile up. Without expiry dates the register fills with accepted risk nobody remembers accepting.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: These are habits I keep when I work on controls and evidence. They are not a checklist from any one engagement. Start from the question, then work backwards. I write down what an auditor would ask and trace it back to the system that could answer it. That finds missing evidence faster than reading the standard top to bottom. Name one owner, even when it is awkward. I would rather have an owner who objects early than a shared owner who is surprised later. Test the evidence, not only the control. I try to answer a question from the store with nobody helping.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: If it takes a conversation, the evidence is not ready. Say what the control does not cover. Writing the limits down in the register protects the owner and keeps the auditor’s scope honest. Treat a gap as normal news. If people are afraid to report one, they will hide it. I ask for gaps early and reward the people who raise them. The longer account of how I run a program from first conversation to handover, including the audit documents I expect at the end, is in How I Run a Privileged Access Program .

A break-glass account is for the day normal access has failed. It has to work when the PAM platform, the identity provider and the MFA service may all be down, so it cannot lean on any of them. Five habits keep it from turning into a side door: credentials kept apart from standing accounts, every use a logged event, an alert on any sign-in or checkout, a written justification, and rotation the same day. Test it on a calendar. An emergency account nobody has tried since it was set up is a guess, and a guess is a poor control.

Emergency access exists to keep incident response moving. Without controls on when it could be invoked, break-glass credentials were also the easiest path around normal approval, and nobody could tell the difference after the fact. The design has to hold up against two opposite failures. If emergency access is hard to reach, people lose hours during an outage, or they quietly keep a shared admin login that nobody governs. If it is easy to reach and quiet to use, it becomes the route people take whenever approval feels slow.
Three properties cover both: it works when everything else is down, it is loud when it is used, and every use is closed out afterwards.
“Break-glass” is not one account. Each layer that can lock people out needs its own way back in, and each has a different owner and a different fallback.

Type — What it gets you back into — Why it stands apart Identity provider or cloud tenant emergency accounts — Administration of the tenant when normal admins cannot sign in — Cloud-only, not federated and not synchronized, so an outage of federation or of the on-premises directory does not touch it PAM platform recovery — The vault and its admin console when the platform is degraded or its own sign-in is broken — A vault cannot hold the only key to itself.

The recovery credential lives outside it, in sealed storage Infrastructure local admin — Servers, hypervisors and databases when directory sign-in fails — A local account on the machine works even if the directory does not.

It is normally vaulted and rotated, with a sealed copy for the day the vault is unreachable Directory and domain — The directory every other system trusts, so it can be repaired or restored — Everything else signs in through it, so its recovery path cannot sign in through it Network devices — Firewalls, switches and routers when central authentication is unreachable — Local or console accounts, used over a management path that does not cross the network being repaired Keep the list short. Every extra emergency account is another spare key, and every one needs an owner, a reason and a drill.

h: Do not depend on what might be down
x: The question I ask about every emergency route is: what has to be working for this to work? If the answer includes the thing that just failed, the route is not an emergency route. If this is down — What goes wrong — What the design does The PAM platform — The recovery credential is inside the thing being recovered — Recovery credentials for the platform are held in sealed, offline storage with two custodians The identity provider — Federated or synchronized admin accounts cannot sign in — Emergency accounts live in the cloud tenant itself.

h: Do not depend on what might be down
x: Microsoft’s guidance lists a federation or identity provider outage as a reason for them The MFA provider — Admins cannot complete the second factor, or their registered devices are unavailable — A different, phishing-resistant method from the one daily admins use, and no tie to one person’s phone Conditional access — A policy that requires a compliant device or a named location can block the very account meant for the emergency — The accounts sit in a group that is excluded from policies that block or restrict sign-in, and a test after every policy change proves it One person or one path — The only keyholder is on leave, or the only network path is the one that failed — More than one custodian, and a check that the route works over at least two network paths that do not share a failure

When the vault itself cannot be reached, the credentials that restart the chain come from sealed, offline storage. The aim is that opening it takes two people and leaves a trace. Split custody or dual control. Either two halves of the secret are held by two people, or two keys are needed to open the container. No single person can use it alone. Tamper-evident and in separate places. Microsoft’s guidance calls for fireproof safes in secure, separate locations, with combinations changed regularly and whenever someone with access leaves. Opening it is an event.

It goes in a custody log with names, time and incident reference, and it triggers the same close-out as any other use: justification, rotation, a fresh sealed copy. Only what restarts the chain. The sealed set holds what is needed to get the platform and the identity layer back, and nothing more. Kept in step with the vault. A sealed copy that no longer matches the live secret fails at the worst moment. Refreshing it is part of rotation, and the drill checks it.

A naming convention, approved and written down. It makes clear that the account is an emergency account, so alert rules, reports and reviewers recognize it straight away. It is tied to a role and a purpose. It is not tied to a person. No link to an individual. Microsoft’s guidance says not to associate these accounts with any individual user, not to connect them to employee-supplied devices such as phones, and to make sure nobody has registered MFA or self-service password reset to a personal device. Two or more accounts, cloud-only.

For the tenant, the guidance says to create two or more emergency access accounts, use the onmicrosoft.com domain, and keep them unfederated and unsynchronized. Phishing-resistant sign-in that differs from daily admins. The guidance recommends a passkey (FIDO2) and offers certificate-based authentication where a PKI already exists. It adds that the method should differ from the one the normal administrator accounts use. Permanent and active, with no expiry. In Privileged Identity Management the guidance asks for the Global Administrator assignment to be permanent active, not eligible.

It also says the credential must not expire or fall under automated clean-up for lack of use, which matters for an account that is dormant by design. A designated secure workstation. The guidance asks that people using these accounts do so from a designated secure workstation or a privileged access workstation.

This is the cycle every break-glass credential goes through. The credential sleeps in the vault. An incident wakes it, it is used under watch, and it is put back to sleep with a new secret. The dots follow one use of the credential: invoked, approved or taken by the sealed fast path, used, closed out, rotated and returned. The bars show what runs alongside it. Break-glass credentials live apart from standing accounts, every invocation is a distinct, logged event, and the credential is rotated the same day and returned to the vault dormant.

Declare the emergency A person in a named role says that normal access has failed and gives the reason, with an incident reference. Nobody is handed break-glass access because they asked politely. Guardrail Only named roles may declare Evidence Incident reference and stated reason

Approve, or take the fast path Normally a named approver says yes, and the credential is released. If the approval tooling is itself down, the fast path applies: two custodians open the sealed copy together, and the approval is recorded as soon as tooling is back. Guardrail Fast path needs two people Evidence Approval record or custody log entry

h: Approve, or take the fast path
x: Invoke The checkout or the unsealing is a distinct, logged event. It is never a quiet reuse of a standing account. Any sign-in or checkout raises an alert to the on-call person and to security. Guardrail Alert on any use Evidence Alert record and log entry

Use it, under watch The person works from a secure workstation, stays inside the incident, and the session is recorded where the platform can record it. Where it cannot, the person keeps a timed note of each action so the review has something to check against the system logs. Guardrail Use limited to the incident and a time box Evidence Session recording or timed action notes

Close out with a justification The person writes down why normal access was not enough, what was done and what the outcome was. A missing justification becomes an open finding that somebody chases. Guardrail No justification, open finding Evidence Justification linked to the incident

Rotate and return The credential is rotated the same day. The new secret is checked with a test sign-in, the sealed copy is refreshed, and the credential goes back to the vault dormant until the next incident. Guardrail Same-day rotation, then a test sign-in Evidence Rotation record with time

Review within a fixed time Someone who did not use the credential reads the logs against the justification within the agreed window. An advisory check flags usage that matches normal-hours, repeat-user patterns, so the reviewer looks hardest where use looks routine and not urgent. The check advises and a person decides. Guardrail Reviewer is independent of the user Evidence Signed review with findings

h: Alerting, and checking the alerts work
x: Microsoft’s guidance is to configure alerts for every use of an emergency access account and to capture sign-in and audit logs for review. Its worked example uses Azure Monitor with a threshold of greater than zero and critical severity, and it says Microsoft Sentinel or other tools can do the same job and send email and SMS to administrators. The same rule applies to the other types: any checkout, unsealing or sign-in raises an alert. An alert that has quietly stopped is worse than none, because people believe they are covered. So I add a second layer that watches the first: A scheduled test event.

h: Alerting, and checking the alerts work
x: The drill sign-in, or a synthetic one, must produce an alert. If the alert does not arrive, that is a finding, raised the same day. A missing-heartbeat rule. If the expected test event is not seen in the log store, something upstream has broken, and that raises its own alert. More than one route. Alerts go out over channels that do not share a failure mode, such as email and SMS, and they do not rely only on the systems that might be down. Logs outside the platform. Records go to a store that the platform’s own admins cannot edit. Security monitoring knows about drills.

h: Alerting, and checking the alerts work
x: Microsoft’s validation steps include making sure monitoring staff are aware when account-check activity is under way, so a drill does not start a real incident.

h: Drills: how often, and what they prove
x: For the tenant accounts, Microsoft’s guidance says to validate at regular intervals and for key changes, at least every 90 days, for example every quarter. It also names triggers such as a change in IT staff or a change in the organization’s subscriptions. I use the same rhythm for the other types, as my own choice and not as something that document prescribes. A drill checks — If it fails, you learn The credential signs in and can do administrative work under today’s policies — A policy change, expiry or clean-up job has broken it.

h: Drills: how often, and what they prove
x: You found out on a quiet day Authorized people can find and open the sealed copy, with two of them present — The custody list is out of date, or a keyholder cannot be reached The alert arrives, at the right people, in the time you expect — The pipeline has a gap, or the wrong people are on the list The use is logged and reviewable — Events are missing, or the log store is not receiving them Rotation and the sealed-copy refresh work end to end — The sealed copy would have been stale in a real emergency The documented process is current and the people are trained — The runbook describes a system that has since changed A drill shows that the route works.

h: Drills: how often, and what they prove
x: It says nothing about whether incident response itself is any good, and I keep those two exercises separate.

I treat break-glass as a process to be onboarded under the organization’s policy, the same as any other privileged access. That means: The password policy is reviewed and refined for these accounts, which are used rarely and by people under pressure. Naming conventions are approved and documented. Vaulting security is documented, with business approval. High availability and disaster recovery are considered from the start. When everything runs in the cloud, the emergency route must not sit on the same dependency as the thing it recovers. The process, the custody list and the drill record are written down where the next person will find them.

The identity provider is down. Admins cannot sign in to the PAM platform, which uses that provider. The on-call engineer declares the incident and gives the reason. The approval tool sits behind the same provider, so the fast path applies. Two custodians open the sealed recovery credential together and log it. An alert reaches the on-call person and security as soon as the credential is used. The engineer restores sign-in from a secure workstation, and the session is recorded.

The engineer writes the justification: what failed, what was done, what was changed. The recovery credential is rotated the same day, tested with a sign-in and returned to sealed storage with a fresh copy. A reviewer who was not involved checks the log against the justification within the agreed window. The custody log, alert, recording, rotation record and review are kept together as the evidence for that use.

It works on day one and is never tried again. A policy change, a departed keyholder or a clean-up job breaks it, and nobody finds out until the emergency. The recovery credential is inside the thing it recovers. The vault holds the only copy of the vault’s own recovery secret. Clean-up jobs disable the dormant account. The fast path becomes the normal path.

If approval is slow, people reach for the glass. The advisory check is there to catch that pattern, and slow approval is the thing to fix. Sealed copies drift. The vault secret is rotated and the sealed copy is left behind. Custody goes stale. People leave or change roles and the list, the combinations and the training are not updated. Too many accounts with too much power. Each extra account is one more thing to watch. Everything on one cloud dependency. The platform and the route to recover it can fail together if they share a region or a provider service.
A drill that only reads the procedure. Nobody signs in, nobody opens the seal, and the drill proves nothing.

Cloud identities hold far more access than they use. That gap is the main thing a cloud entitlement program works on, and each cloud already records the usage data needed to measure it. Reviewing one role or one policy at a time misses combinations. What an identity can really do is the union of everything attached to it, plus whatever it can reach through trust links to other accounts. Every cut goes to an owner for approval, ships with a rollback, and is backed by policy as code and organization-level guardrails, so the excess does not return.

Cloud permissions pile up. A role is created for a project and given broad rights so the launch does not slip. A person changes teams and keeps their old access. A pipeline’s service account gets one more policy each time a deploy fails. Nobody takes anything away, because removing access can break something and nobody can say for sure that it will not. Four kinds of identity sit in that pile: people, workloads, federated identities that arrive through a corporate directory or an outside provider, and service accounts that exist for one job. Each cloud models them in its own way.

The names, the policy languages and the ways of attaching permissions all differ, so a view built for one cloud tells you little about the next. Two problems come out of this. The first is size. Granted permissions are much larger than used permissions, and that gap is attack surface. The second is shape. When policies are reviewed one at a time, combinations go unseen. An identity can hold two permissions that each look reasonable and that together let it change its own access, or reach data that another account controls. The real entitlement is the union of every policy attached to the identity.
In the program this page describes, that was the starting point: policies reviewed singly, with risky combinations found late or by chance.

Three words carry most of the confusion in this area, so I define them early and keep them fixed. Granted is what is written in the policies attached to an identity. Effective is what the identity can do once everything is combined: direct policies, group or role membership, resource policies, permission boundaries, organization-level guardrails, deny rules and trust relationships. Effective permissions are what an attacker inherits. Used is what the logs show the identity did over a stated window. The work is the gap between effective and used, and the paths hidden inside effective. The three major clouds each publish usage data that helps.

Two broad policies give write access to every storage bucket and every queue in the account. The role can also create roles and attach policies to them, which is a path to more access. A trust link lets a second account assume it, left over from a migration that finished long ago. The owner field is empty.

Write access covers one bucket prefix and one queue, which is what the logs showed. The ability to create roles and attach policies is gone. The trust link is removed after the owning team confirmed the migration was over. A named team owns the role, and the change sits in version control with its rollback. Three checks sat between the logs and the cut. The first window was 90 days, and the team mentioned a quarterly job, so we widened the window and held that permission until the owner confirmed.

The permission to pass a role to another service does not appear in the usage data, so we reviewed it by hand. And the rollback copy was restored once in a test account before the change went to production.

A cleanup that ends is a cleanup that reverses. Three mechanisms work together. Policy as code. Policies live in a repository and ship through a pipeline. AWS describes custom policy checks in IAM Access Analyzer that compare an updated policy with the existing one and report new access, or confirm that specified access is not allowed. Wired into the pipeline, a change that adds access stops there for review. Organization-level boundaries. Service control policies in AWS Organizations do not grant permissions. They set the outer limit of what can be granted, so an undesired permission cannot take effect even when an attached policy allows it.

They govern principals inside the organization, and they do not apply to the management account. Google Cloud offers deny policies, which override allow policies. Both are blunt tools, so I write each one narrowly, with a named exception route. A rhythm of review. Entra access reviews, with owners or managers as reviewers, give a scheduled way to confirm human and service principal access. For the rest, I rerun the analysis on a calendar and compare it with the last snapshot.

Credentials end up everywhere: vaults, config files, chat, wikis, pipeline variables. The problem is rarely a missing tool. It is that nobody owns the whole picture. A platform fixes that with three things: a short service catalog, one named owner for every credential, and a lifecycle that runs the same way for all of them. The best credential is one that does not exist. Where a short-lived identity will do, use it before you vault a long-lived secret.

“Credential” covers a lot: passwords, API keys, SSH keys, tokens, database logins, cloud access keys and the secrets behind service accounts. In most companies each team grew its own way of handling them. One team uses a vault, another uses encrypted files, a third keeps them in pipeline variables, and some still sit in a shared document. Nothing is obviously broken until someone asks simple questions. Where does this credential live? Who owns it? When did it last change? Who has read it? If the answers take days to find, there is no control, only hope.
The fix is to treat credential management as a service with users, a menu and rules, and not as a collection of tools.

Start by writing down what the platform offers, who it is for, and what it does not cover. A short catalog is easier to adopt than a long one, and it gives each request a clear place to go. Service — For — What it does Privileged access for people — Admins, database owners, engineers on call — Approved, recorded sessions to servers, databases and cloud accounts, with no standing admin rights Secrets for applications — Developers and platform teams — Applications fetch secrets at runtime from one store. Nothing is copied into code or config.

Short-lived and dynamic credentials — Applications and pipelines — Credentials generated on demand that expire by themselves, so a leak has a short life Service account management — System owners — Every machine account has an owner, a rotation policy and a record of where it is used Inventory and reporting — Security, risk and audit — One view of what exists, who owns it, its age and its access history Decide the boundaries early. Certificates, for example, often have their own lifecycle and owners. If they are out of scope for the first release, say so in the catalog.

Four kinds of requester ask the platform for access. The platform is the only place that stores secrets, applies policy, rotates them and writes the log. Around it sit the systems a company already runs: a directory for sign-in and MFA, a service desk for approvals, and a SIEM for detection. The dots show a secret request traveling from a requester, through policy and the vault, to the system it protects. The named products are examples of each role, not an endorsement; any equivalent directory, service desk or SIEM fits the same slot.

Whatever the credential type, it should move through the same six stages. The ring shows the loop, and the owner and policy set at the start stay attached the whole way. The same loop applies to a database password, an API key or a service account. Retire is part of the loop: a credential nobody uses should not outlive the system it served.

The password sits in a config file in a code repository. About fifteen people have seen it over the years. It has not changed since launch, because nobody is sure what would break. Nobody can say who actually owns it.

A tier describes blast radius. A credential belongs in the highest tier of anything it can change or mint access to, wherever it happens to be stored. Each tier gets a fixed set of controls: storage, rotation, access path, monitoring, approval and session recording. They get stronger towards Tier 0, and a credential that is valid in one tier is never valid in another. PAM products are sold as capabilities such as vaulting, session management and just-in-time access, not as tiers. Work out what each tier needs first, then see which tools supply it.

Most organizations have a vault. Far fewer can say which of their credentials are worth the most to an attacker, and which controls those credentials get. So the same standard ends up applied to a helpdesk password and to the account that administers the identity provider. Either the strong controls are too expensive to use everywhere, or the weak ones sit in front of things that matter. The usual attack path is short. Someone phishes a laptop, finds a credential that also works somewhere more valuable, and keeps moving. Nothing in that story needs a clever exploit.

It needs one credential that is valid in more places than it should be. Tiering is the habit of asking, for every credential, how far it could go if it were stolen, and then drawing a hard line at each step so that it cannot go further. Friction has a cost too. If every credential needs two approvers and a hardware key, people route around the process. If none do, the account that can rewrite your identity system is protected like a shared mailbox. Tiers are how you spend the friction where it buys the most.

h: Where the tier idea comes from
x: The Tier 0, 1, 2 language comes from Microsoft's Active Directory tier model, which was designed to contain unauthorized escalation of privilege in an on-premises Windows Server Active Directory environment. Microsoft's current guidance, the enterprise access model, builds on that model and widens it to cover on-premises, multiple clouds, internal and external users, and more. It did not throw the idea away. It renamed and split the tiers so they still make sense outside a single directory. In Microsoft's mapping, Tier 0 becomes the control plane: identity systems, centralized access enforcement and, where it is the only option, network controls.

h: Where the tier idea comes from
x: Tier 1 is split into a management plane for enterprise-wide IT management and a data and workload plane for per-workload management. Tier 2 becomes access pathways for users and for applications and APIs. Microsoft's wording differs a little between pages, so I read the mapping as a direction. One sentence from the architecture page is the reason Tier 0 gets the most attention: compromise of the control plane often enables indirect control of all other planes. Microsoft's privileged access strategy also defines three security levels: enterprise, specialized and privileged.

h: Where the tier idea comes from
x: At the privileged level, a person does not do sensitive work and everyday productivity tasks on the same account or device. I use that as the access-path rule for Tier 0. Two things here are my own. I use four tiers, with Tier 3 as a home for low-impact credentials. And I place individual credentials into tiers, where Microsoft's pages talk about planes and access pathways. The credential-level placement and the control set are my working method.

Read the diagram one row at a time. A request starts at the left, passes the controls on its tier's path, and only then reaches what it can change on the right. Tier 0 has four gates, Tier 1 three, Tier 2 two and Tier 3 one. Every row writes to the same audit log, kept outside the platform being audited. Each moving dot is a credential in use. It only reaches the right-hand side after passing every control on its own row. No arrow runs from one row to another, so a Tier 2 credential has no path into Tier 0.

The gates show the shape of the control set, not a product. Tier 0 holds the identity control plane: domain controllers, certificate authorities, the PAM vaults, and the admin plane of whatever runs your single sign-on. A cloud identity provider's global admin role is Tier 0 even with no server rack behind it. Tier 1 is the application, cloud and CI/CD estate. Tier 2 is workstation and helpdesk administration, the most common way in. Tier 3 is everyone else, the largest attack surface by count.

Class — What it is — Where it usually lands — What decides the tier Human privileged — Admin accounts used by people: directory, cloud, database, helpdesk — Tier 0, 1 or 2 — What the account can administer. This is an illustration, not a specific event. A pipeline holds a cloud key to deploy an application. First placement looks easy: a cloud key used by CI/CD, so Tier 1. Then the mint test. The role behind the key can create roles and attach policies in the cloud account, so the key can give itself anything, including admin rights over the account's identity layer. Its real tier is Tier 0 until the permissions change.

The key is long-lived and sits in a pipeline variable that every maintainer can read. The role was made broad so deployments would stop failing. Nobody can say which tier it belongs to. It is never reviewed because the pipeline works.

The pipeline gets short-lived credentials through a workload identity and no stored key remains. The role is cut down to deploy actions. Role creation is removed, so the credential drops to Tier 1. The owner, tier and expiry sit in the inventory. A change to the role triggers a tier check.

h: Where the PAM market fits the tiers
x: Tiers describe credentials. PAM products are packaged as capabilities, and the two do not line up one to one. Gartner defines PAM as a set of tools to control access and secure accounts that provide an elevated level of technical access, for human and machine accounts. Its capability list includes vaulting and rotation, session management, just-in-time privilege and provisioning, secrets management, command control, account discovery and onboarding, and privilege elevation. Those are the building blocks, and each tier needs a different mix.

Enterprise PAM suites such as CyberArk and BeyondTrust are the usual starting point. Mid-market. Standard compliance needs without heavy overhead. The owner proposes, someone else approves, and the record shows both. Review the standard too. If every team asks for an exception to the same control, the control is wrong or the front door is too slow. Exceptions have owners and end dates. Anything that cannot meet its tier's controls, such as a legacy application needing a static password, goes on a register with a plan and a date. Measure coverage and drift.

Useful measures are the share of known credentials classified, credentials with no owner, credentials above their tier, Tier 0 systems still reachable by a direct path, and the age of the oldest unrotated secret.

Tier 0 is drawn too small. Teams list the domain controllers and forget the cloud identity provider's admin roles, the pipelines that deploy to the identity layer, or the vault. The vault stops at Tier 0. Many estates have a vault at the top and little below it, yet Tier 1 and Tier 2 are where a first foothold usually lands. Classification is done once. A Tier 1 credential can pick up permissions and become Tier 0 unnoticed. Review on change, not only on a calendar. The gate is a single point of failure.

If the vault or approval system is down during an incident, the response cannot be to wait for it. That is what a tested break-glass path is for. See break-glass access . Tiers turn into org charts. Tier 0 is for credentials that can mint other credentials, not a list of senior people. A product gets mistaken for a tier. A tool bought for one tier gets assumed to cover the rest. Temporary credentials stay forever. Accounts made to bridge a migration get forgotten because they were never meant to last. AI agents get standing access.
An agent that reviews access or manages secrets needs its own tier, scope and expiry. See AI agent credential sharing .

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: These are habits from how I run this kind of work. They are not a report on any one project. I ask what a credential can mint before I ask where it lives. Location is easy to see and misleading. Reach decides the tier. I finish Tier 0 before I start the rest. A half-built gate in every tier gives false comfort. A complete gate on the control plane is a smaller area I can defend properly. I keep the number of tiers small. When a team asks for a fifth tier, I look for a missing control in one of the four.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: I test the boundary by trying to cross it. Reading a policy proves little. Taking a low-tier credential and attempting to use it in a higher tier shows what is real. I write the tier definitions on one page and get them approved by the people they bind. If only security has read them, they last until the first incident review. I judge tools after I have written what each tier needs. Then I try two or three candidates on a small slice. That settles more than a comparison table. I give every temporary credential an expiry the day it is created.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: Cleanup backlogs do not get done. I test break-glass before go-live. It is part of the Tier 0 design, so it gets built and tried before the gate goes live. Admin rights granted as standing role membership outlive the task that justified them. Audits then depend on people remembering to take access back. The fix is elevation with two limits: a short window and a narrow scope. Each request opens a window, and the window closes on its own. I size the window from what people really did with the role. An advisory step can propose scope and duration, but the requester and the approver still decide.

Administrative rights were granted as standing role membership. Someone needed access for a migration, got added to a role, and stayed in it long after the migration ended. Every audit relied on people remembering to revoke what they no longer needed, and remembering is a weak control. A privileged account that is always on is always worth stealing. MITRE ATT&CK lists Valid Accounts (T1078) as a technique that adversaries use for initial access, persistence, privilege escalation and defense evasion. A standing admin role hands them all four for as long as the account exists.
Shrinking the hours in which an account is privileged shrinks what a stolen credential can do.

h: Two terms that get mixed up
x: Just-in-time (JIT) is about time. Privilege is activated when a task needs it and ends when the window ends. JEA has a precise meaning at Microsoft: Just Enough Administration, a PowerShell feature. You write role capability files ( .psrc ) that list the cmdlets, functions and commands a role may run, and a session configuration ( .pssc ) that says who can connect, which roles they get and which identity the session runs as. Users connect to a constrained endpoint. The session can run as a virtual account, which Microsoft describes as a temporary local account that is destroyed when the session ends.

h: Two terms that get mixed up
x: In this case study the title says “Just-Enough-Access”, which is the wider idea: give the smallest scope that does the job, on any platform. I write “JEA” only when I mean Microsoft’s feature, and I write “just-enough scope” for the general idea. The two work well together. JIT limits when, and just-enough scope limits what.
