Those belong to the credential platform, not to this flow.

h: The same idea in different places
x: Kubernetes — In my approach, short-lived access bound to a narrow role, with cluster-wide admin reserved for a small, approved set of cases. — Cluster roles can be broader than anyone intended. Review what each role really allows before you size a window for it. A vendor-neutral summary comes from the UK National Cyber Security Center. Instead of using a credential to reach an administration interface, the administrator uses it to request access, and if the request is approved a temporary credential is issued.

h: The same idea in different places
x: The NCSC also says that shortening how long an administration credential can be used cuts the attacker’s window if one is stolen.

Ask for a task, not a role The requester names the target, the task, the ticket or change number and how long they think they need. “Admin on everything for a week” is not a valid request. Microsoft’s PIM has a ticket field, but its documentation says it is information only and does not check the number against a ticketing system. So the service desk does the checking. Guardrail No open ticket, no request Evidence Request record

h: Ask for a task, not a role
x: Prove who they are, properly Sign-in goes through single sign-on, with multi-factor authentication and conditional access. The details matter here. PIM can require MFA on activation, and it can require a Conditional Access authentication context, for example a specific authentication strength or a compliant device. If someone has just reauthenticated for one activation, Microsoft says they are not asked again within ten minutes for other eligible roles. Guardrail No MFA, no activation Evidence Sign-in log

Get an advisory proposal A policy-aware assistant reads the request and proposes a scope and a duration, using what the role has really been used for. It is a suggestion. The requester can change it, and the approver sees it next to the request. The proposal can never go above the maximum the policy sets for that role. Guardrail Proposal capped by policy, humans decide Evidence Proposal and final choice, both recorded

Approve by policy, or by a person Roles with low risk and a pre-agreed use can be approved by policy. Anything touching production or the identity systems needs a named person. Approvals flow through the service desk (ServiceNow in my setup). PIM itself says approvers cannot approve their own activation requests, and that an unapproved request expires after 24 hours and has to be submitted again. I apply the same rule to every platform: the requester is never the approver. Guardrail Separation of duties Evidence Approver, time, reason

h: Approve by policy, or by a person
x: Open the window The eligible assignment is activated, or the group membership is added with an expiry, or the broker session starts. The window carries its own end time from the first second. PIM’s activation maximum can be set between 1 and 24 hours per role. Guardrail Smallest role that does the task, end time set at the start Evidence Activation record with start and end

Work, and leave a trail Everything the person does is logged, and on brokered sessions recorded. Logs go to the SIEM so that the people who hold the privilege cannot edit the record of using it. Guardrail Logs stored outside the elevation tool Evidence Session record or audit log tied to the ticket

Close it and look back When the timer ends or the task is marked complete, the access is removed by the system. A follow-up ticket is never needed. Afterwards I look at windows that closed with no privileged action in them, because they tell me the role or the window was too big. Guardrail Expiry enforced by the system, not by memory Evidence Expiry event and the review of unused windows

h: When the work runs past the window
x: Change windows overrun. I handle this as a fresh request with fresh approval, never as a silent extension. The requester says why more time is needed, and the approver can see how long the first window ran. For an activation that is running out, the simple rule is to request again.

h: When the elevation path is down
x: The identity provider, the service desk or the broker can be unavailable at the worst moment. Break glass stays available for exactly this. Microsoft’s guidance for Entra is two or more cloud-only emergency accounts, made permanently active and not eligible, with phishing-resistant sign-in, alerts on every use, and a check at least every 90 days. The NCSC says to protect the break-glass process carefully. I cover the design in Break-Glass Emergency Access Design .

h: Accounts that cannot be elevated just in time
x: A scheduled task or a service account has no person to request anything at 3 a.m. Forcing it through this flow only produces a service account with permanent approval. These identities go to the credential platform instead, where they get an owner, a rotation policy or a short-lived credential. The two case studies fit together: Credential Management Platform Strategy for the machine side and Non-Human Identity at Scale for the scale problem.

A longer default window is a risk decision, and it has a named owner. The advisory step is governed like any other policy input. Its rules, caps and changes are documented and approved, and its proposals are logged beside the final decision. Exceptions have owners and end dates. Anything left as standing access sits on a register and is reviewed on a rhythm.

Approval fatigue. If approvers see hundreds of requests a week, they start approving without reading. Pre-agreed roles can go through policy, so people only look at the risky ones. Windows set wrong in both directions. Too short and people get cut off in the middle of a change. Too long and the window is standing access with a new name. Eligible becomes the new standing. If everyone is eligible for everything, the list of eligible people is the list of targets. Eligible accounts still need strong sign-in and regular review. The elevation path becomes a dependency.

When the identity provider or service desk is down, nobody can fix anything. This is why the fallback has to be built and tested first. JEA endpoints with loose roles. Microsoft warns against wildcards in role capabilities and against allowing commands such as Start-Process, and notes that a local administrator can change a JEA configuration. A JEA endpoint is only as tight as its role file. Legacy systems with no concept of expiry. Some platforms cannot remove access on a timer. A broker session or a scripted removal can close the gap, and the rest goes on the exceptions register. Adoption friction.
Engineers who used to have instant access now wait. If the wait is long or the form is long, they will look for ways around it.

I start where the platform already does the work. Cloud and directory roles first, because activation, approval and expiry exist there. Those early results buy trust for the harder platforms.

x: I keep the advisory step advisory. It proposes, people decide, and I log both. I also look at where people disagree with it, because that is where the policy needs work. A migration moves more than accounts. The old tool also carries controls, approvals, integrations and habits, and some of them were never written down. I start by analyzing what the current tool does, what it fails to do and what is inside it. Then I run discovery and get the plan signed off before anything moves. Waves follow dependency, risk, access criticality and rollback readiness. At cutover every secret is rotated, because whatever sat in the old vault has to be treated as known to the people who administered it.

A privileged access migration has to preserve controls, user journeys, integrations and operational continuity. Moving the accounts is the easy part. The hard part is everything around them: the approval that fires before a checkout, the nightly script that reads a password from the old tool’s API, the alert someone relies on, the administrator who knows which safe to open at 2 a.m. The old tool has usually been running for years. People built on it without telling anyone. If you only copy the inventory you will move the accounts and lose the behavior.

Most of my planning work is about finding that behavior early and deciding, on paper, what happens to each piece of it. I led the analysis of the ERPM PAM tool and the capability mapping for the target-state decision. The method below is what that work taught me to do every time.

h: Start with the tool you already have
x: When an organization already has a tool and wants to move to a new one, I do not start with the new one. I start with three questions about the old one. What does it do today? Features, integrations, and how people really use it, which is often different from how it was designed. What is it failing to do? The gaps that made the organization want to move. These become requirements for the target, so they are worth writing down in the owners’ own words. What is inside it? The inventory of accounts, safes or folders, policies and owners.

h: Start with the tool you already have
x: I treat this as a claim to be checked, not as a fact. The answers feed a capability map: one row per thing the old tool does, and what the target does about it. That map is what the target-state decision and the later control-equivalence checks are built on.

I split the inventory into five classes, because each one migrates differently and each one has a different person to ask. Class — Examples — The question I ask — What makes it tricky Human privileged — Domain, local and root admin accounts, database administrators — Who actually uses it, and how often? — People have habits and saved sessions. Workflow and approval rules have to match or people work around them. Service and application — Service accounts, application and database logins, API keys — What reads this, and what breaks if it changes? — Changing the value can stop a job.

This is where hidden dependencies live. Shared — Accounts used by a team, vendor or help desk — Who is in the group, and who is it really? — Without individual accountability, the session record is the only evidence of who did what. Machine — SSH keys, certificates, tokens, secrets used by pipelines and workloads — Could this be short-lived instead of stored? — Some stores hold them in fields nobody tracks. Some cannot accept a rotated value.

Break glass — Emergency accounts for when sign-in or the platform is down — Does it work if everything else is broken? — It must follow organization policy and be tested, because it is the way back in during a failed cutover.

h: Discovery: finding what nobody wrote down
x: The exported inventory tells you what the tool believes. Discovery tells you what is true. I use several sources and compare them, because each one is wrong in a different way. Source — What it shows — How it misleads The old tool’s own account list — What was onboarded, with owners and policies — Owners have left, and accounts were added and never removed. Usage and audit logs of the old tool — Who checked out what, when it last happened, which API clients called it — Quiet accounts may still matter once a quarter or once a year.

h: Discovery: finding what nobody wrote down
x: Scans of servers, directory and network devices — Privileged accounts that exist but were never vaulted — A scan finds accounts, not the reason they exist. Scheduled tasks, scripts and pipeline code — Jobs that call the old tool or hard-code a credential — Code search misses what lives in someone’s head or on a laptop. Tickets and approval history — Real request patterns and who approves — People raise tickets differently from how the process says. Interviews with owners — Purpose, business impact and the workarounds — People forget, and some things were set up by someone who has moved on.

For every credential that something other than a person uses, I record who or what reads it, how (API call, agent, script, scheduled task or a hard-coded copy), how often, what stops working if the value changes, and who can fix it. That record decides the wave a credential goes into and whether it can be rotated at cutover. A hard-coded use is not a reason to skip the credential. It is a work item for its owner, with a date, before the wave.

Before anything moves, every row of the capability map gets one decision. The matrix below is illustrative. The capabilities are typical, and the decisions are examples of the kind of result I record, not findings from a real estate.

The plan has two halves. First, plan and prove: understand the old tool, discover, decide and sign off, then build a small proof in Dev. Then move and retire: rehearse in pre-production, go live in waves, rotate, and switch the old tool off. Rollback stays open across the second half. A database service account is owned by the infrastructure team. Nobody has checked it out in a long time. It looks safe to move early and rotate on day one.

h: What discovery shows and what I do
x: A scheduled job reads it through the old tool’s API every night. I record the job and its owner, and ask the owner to repoint it to the target before the wave. The account moves in the same wave as the job, and is rotated after the job has run once successfully.

A wave is a set of accounts that move together, with a date, an owner and a way back. I order them using four criteria. Criterion — The question — Effect on order Dependency — What reads this, and does it move in the same wave? — Things that depend on each other go together. Risk — What is the exposure today, and what could a bad move cause? — High exposure argues for early, but only once the route is proven.

Access criticality — How badly does the business suffer if this access fails? — The most critical access goes after a rehearsal, with an owner present. Rollback readiness — Can we go back, and have we tried? — No wave without a tested way back. In practice the first wave is small and low in criticality, so the team learns on something forgiving. Break glass is ready before the first production wave, because it is the way back in if something goes wrong.

Parallel running. Both tools are live for a while. The rule I keep is that one tool is the source of truth for any given account at any given time, and everybody knows which. Two tools each changing the same password is a recipe for lockouts. Cutover. For each wave the accounts are verified in the target, the owners repoint their consumers, the old tool’s entries for those accounts go read-only, and the owner accepts the wave. Rollback criteria. I write them before the wave, in plain language, with the decision maker named.

Typical triggers: A critical dependency cannot read its credential and cannot be fixed inside the agreed window. Sessions cannot be brokered for a critical group of systems. The approval or ticket integration fails, so access cannot be granted in a controlled way. The break-glass test fails. Rollback is simple until secrets are rotated, because the old vault still holds values that work. After rotation the old values are dead, so a rollback means restoring or re-setting them.
For that reason I agree the point where the rollback window closes with the owners, and I put it right after acceptance and the first successful run of the dependent jobs.

The old vault’s secrets should be treated as exposed to the old administrators. They could read them, the old backups hold them, and export files from the migration may have copies. Nobody needs to have done anything wrong for that to be true. It is a question of who could have seen them. So each secret is changed after it lands in the target, and then the export files and old copies are removed and recorded as removed. For people’s memorised passwords, NIST SP 800-63B advises against forced periodic changes without evidence of compromise.
Vaulted privileged credentials are different: the tool sets them, nobody types them, and a change costs almost nothing.

Everything now sits on cloud, and the platform will hold the keys to a lot. Before a production wave I want to know the target can lose a component without losing the service, that a second region exists with agreed recovery objectives, that a restore has actually been tried, and that break glass works when the platform or the identity provider does not. NIST SP 800-53 CP-10 expresses the same thing: recover the system to a known state within a time consistent with the recovery objectives.

The old tool is not finished when the last wave moves. Its audit logs and session recordings often have to be kept for a retention period, so I plan who can read them, in what format, where they live and for how long. Remove the old tool’s reach. It had accounts on targets to rotate and log in. Those accounts, and the integrations that used them, are removed. Archive the evidence. Logs and recordings go to an archive with an owner, a read process and a retention date taken from the organization’s own requirements.

NIST SP 800-53 AU-11 asks for records to be retained for an organization-defined period. Where PCI DSS applies, requirement 10.5.1 asks for at least 12 months of audit log history, with the most recent three months immediately available. Check the archive can be read. Machine identities get created faster than anyone records them. The first job is one inventory, with a named owner against every entry and a flag on every entry that has none. A simple score turns that inventory into a queue. I rank on three things: how long since the secret changed, how much it can do, and whether anyone owns it. Evidence of exposure and last use come next. The best fix removes the secret. Where a workload can use a role, federation or a short-lived token, do that before you rotate a static key.

A non-human identity is anything that signs in without a person at the keyboard: a service account, an API key, a token, a certificate, a workload identity, an OAuth app, a bot, and more and more often an AI agent. Each one is a way into a system, and each one raises the same questions as a person’s account. Who is it for? What can it reach? When was it last changed? Who would notice if it were misused? The difference is how they come into being. A developer creates a service account to unblock a release.

A pipeline needs a token, so someone makes one. A vendor integration asks for an OAuth grant, and an admin clicks yes. None of these goes through the process a new employee goes through, and none of them has a manager who changes jobs and hands the account over. So ownership gets lost at handoff, credentials outlive the systems that issued them, and audits fall back on belief. “We think the team rotates these” is a sentence I have heard in more than one review, and it is not evidence.

OWASP’s Non-Human Identities Top 10 puts improper offboarding first, which it describes as inadequate deactivation or removal of non-human identities when they are no longer needed. That is the same failure in different words. I have left out any ratio of machines to people. Figures like that circulate widely, and I could not trace one to a primary source with a method I trust. The program does not depend on the number. It depends on knowing your own inventory.

Kind — Where it tends to live — What usually goes wrong Service accounts — Directories, databases, operating systems, cloud IAM — Created for one project, kept for ten. The password is shared and never changes. API keys and access keys — Cloud accounts, SaaS admin consoles, config files — Copied into code or chat. No expiry, broad scope. Tokens — Pipeline variables, developer machines, repositories — Tied to the person who made it, so it breaks or lingers when they move on. Certificates and keys — Load balancers, services, key stores — Expiry surprises, and private keys copied between environments.

Workload identities — Cloud roles, managed identities, cluster service accounts — Roles that started narrow and grew permission by permission. OAuth apps and integrations — SaaS platforms, identity provider consent screens — Third-party access granted once and never reviewed. Bots and automation — Chat tools, ticketing, scheduled jobs — Run with an admin login because that was quickest. AI agents — Agent platforms, tool servers, developer tooling — Share one key across agents, or act on a person’s delegated token. See One Key, Every Agent . How the credentials themselves are stored, issued and rotated is covered in Credential Management Platform Strategy .
This page picks up one step earlier: finding what exists, deciding who answers for it, and deciding what to fix first.

Five kinds of source tell you what exists. Cloud IAM lists roles, access keys and app registrations. CI/CD systems list pipeline variables and tokens. Code scanning finds secrets sitting in repositories and their history. Vaults know what is stored, when it last rotated and when it was last read. Directories hold the service accounts. Each source sees a different slice, and the same identity often appears in two or three of them under different names. Everything flows into one inventory. From there each record needs an owner, then a score, and then it lands in a queue where someone fixes it.

A re-scan afterwards confirms the fix, and an evidence log keeps who, what and when for every step. The scanning is read-only. Fixing happens in the source system, by the owner. Each dot is one identity: found in a source, merged into the inventory, given an owner, scored and queued. The numbers on the boxes match the first five steps of the workflow below. The dashed lines into the evidence log show that every stage writes to it.

Seven steps. Each has a guardrail, which is the rule that keeps the step honest, and the evidence an auditor can ask to see. Discover from every source you can reach Start with the two or three sources that hold the most: usually cloud IAM, the main vault and the code repositories. Keep a register of sources, with a person who answers for each one, so a gap in coverage is visible and not silent. Guardrail Read-only discovery access, every source has an owner Evidence Source register with last successful scan date

h: Discover from every source you can reach
x: Merge into one inventory Give each identity one record with a few required fields: type, system, environment, created date, last rotated, last used, privilege level, owner and the source that found it. When two sources describe the same identity, merge them. When a record is missing a field, flag it and keep it. A half-filled record is still better than no record. Guardrail Required fields, and incomplete records are flagged, not dropped Evidence Inventory export with field completeness

Assign a named owner An owner is a person or a team that will answer for the identity, change it and retire it. Where nobody claims it, the record goes to the owner of the system it touches, and from there to a review queue with a deadline. Ownership has to be accepted, because being named by someone else does not make a person accountable. Guardrail No owner within the agreed time raises the score and routes to review Evidence Owner acceptance record

Score every identity the same way Use one formula, version it, and store the inputs next to the result so anyone can see why an identity ranks where it does. The factors and a worked example are in the next section. The score orders the work. It says nothing about the quality of a team. Guardrail One versioned formula, inputs kept with the score Evidence Score history per identity

h: Score every identity the same way
x: Fix at the source, in a fixed order Work down the queue. For each identity ask four questions in order. Is it still used? If not, retire it. Can the workload use a role, federation or a short-lived token? If so, replace the secret. Is the access wider than the job needs? Cut it. Is a static secret still unavoidable? Rotate it, and set the next rotation. Retiring comes before rotating, because rotating something nobody uses only adds work. Guardrail Retire first, remove the secret second, rotate last Evidence Change record in the system that owns the identity

h: Fix at the source, in a fixed order
x: Verify, then close A fix is closed when a re-scan shows the change and the owner confirms it. If the owner stays silent, the item escalates. Closing a ticket on someone’s word is how stale findings come back at the next audit. Guardrail Closure needs a re-scan result, and a ticket status alone is not enough Evidence Before and after scan, owner confirmation

Guard the front door The cleanup only holds if new identities arrive through a path that asks for an owner, a purpose and an expiry. Secret scanning on commits keeps new keys out of code. Anything created outside the path shows up in the next scan and counts against the owner of the system. Guardrail Creation path requires owner and expiry, secret scanning on commit Evidence Blocked-commit log, exceptions register

h: Scoring: how I rank the list
x: A flat list of thousands of identities cannot be worked. A short score does the sorting. The model I use on this site has three factors. I keep it small on purpose, because a score people can recompute in their head gets trusted, and one they cannot gets ignored. Factor — How it is calculated — Why it is there Staleness — Days since the credential last changed, divided by 30, capped at 10, then multiplied by 0.55 — A secret that has not changed has had more time to leak and be copied.

h: Scoring: how I rank the list
x: Privilege — Standard counts 1, Elevated 2 and Admin 3.2, then multiplied by 1.6 — It sets the blast radius. The same leak costs far more at Admin. Ownership gap — Add 3.5 if no owner is recorded — With no owner there is nobody to rotate, scope down or retire it. Add the three results, round to a whole number and keep it between 1 and 10. A score of 7 or more counts as high risk, 4 to 6 as medium and below that as low. These weights are starting values for the demonstration, and they are no standard.

h: Scoring: how I rank the list
x: In a real program I would tune them with the data owner and the people who answer for incidents, then freeze the version. Two policies change the result and are easy to explain. Enforcing a 90-day rotation caps the staleness input at 90 days. Requiring an owner within 30 days of creation removes the ownership gap.

This is an illustration with made-up identities. It does not describe a specific event. Input — A: deploy token for a pipeline — B: reporting service account Privilege — Admin, 3.2 × 1.6 = 5.12 — Elevated, 2 × 1.6 = 3.20 Last changed — 400 days. 400 / 30 = 13.3, capped at 10, × 0.55 = 5.50 — 150 days. 150 / 30 = 5, × 0.55 = 2.75 Owner — None, +3.50 — Named team, +0 Total — 14.12, kept at the maximum of 10. High. — 5.95, rounds to 6. Medium.
Now take token A and apply fixes one at a time, to see which one does the work.

Change to token A — Calculation — Score Start — 5.50 + 5.12 + 3.50 = 14.12 — 10, high Assign an owner and enforce 90-day rotation — 1.65 + 5.12 + 0 = 6.77 — 7, still high Also cut Admin down to Elevated — 1.65 + 3.20 + 0 = 4.85 — 5, medium Replace it with a federated, short-lived token, so nothing is stored — 0 + 3.20 + 0 = 3.20 — 3, low The lesson I draw from this is that ownership and rotation cut the score a long way and still left it at 7.

The privilege cut and the removal of the stored secret finished the job. That is why the order in step 5 starts with retiring and replacing, and leaves rotation for last. What the score leaves out matters too. It does not see whether the secret has already been found in code, or whether the identity has been used in the last quarter. Once the inventory is trustworthy I add those two as extra factors. An identity with a known exposure moves to the top whatever its other numbers say.

h: Removing the secret: federation and short-lived tokens
x: Rotation limits how long a stolen secret works. Removing the stored secret removes the thing to steal. Most major platforms now document a way for a workload to prove who it is and receive a credential that expires on its own. Roles on the platform itself. AWS’s IAM guidance says workloads on its compute services should use temporary credentials delivered with an IAM role, and that there is no need to distribute long-lived credentials for an IAM user to workloads running on AWS.

h: Removing the secret: federation and short-lived tokens
x: The same guidance says that where long-term keys cannot be avoided, you should update them when needed, and use last accessed information to find and remove credentials you no longer need. Federation for pipelines and outside workloads. GitHub Actions can request a signed OIDC token for each run and exchange it with a cloud provider for a short-lived access token, so no cloud credential has to be stored as a long-lived GitHub secret. The workflow needs the id-token: write permission, which does not by itself let it write to any resource.

h: Removing the secret: federation and short-lived tokens
x: GitHub also says you must define at least one condition on the token’s claims, so that untrusted repositories cannot request tokens for your cloud resources. The subject claim can narrow that to an environment, a branch or pull requests. Google Cloud describes Workload Identity Federation as a way to authenticate workloads outside Google Cloud without a static service account key. Microsoft Entra documents the same pattern for software outside Azure, including GitHub Actions and Kubernetes workloads. OWASP’s list includes insecure cloud deployment configurations and mentions improperly validated OIDC tokens in that item, so the trust condition is where review effort belongs after the move.

h: Removing the secret: federation and short-lived tokens
x: Workload identity across platforms. SPIFFE defines an ID for a workload in the form spiffe://trust-domain/workload and a verifiable document for it, called an SVID, as either an X.509 certificate or a JWT. The project notes that X.509 is preferred, because tokens are susceptible to replay. Through the Workload API a workload gets its credentials without holding an authentication secret, and the keys are short-lived and rotated automatically.

h: Removing the secret: federation and short-lived tokens
x: SPIRE is the reference implementation: a server issues identities for a trust domain, an agent runs on each node, the agent is attested when it first connects, and each workload is attested by matching its properties to a registration entry. I reach for this when many services across several clusters or clouds need to identify each other. Where everything sits in one cloud, that cloud’s native roles are simpler to run. NSA and CISA’s 2024 cloud identity guidance points the same way.

A reader on LinkedIn, Gelson Monteiro, made the point that Zero Standing Privilege only holds once ownership is enforced, and that finding non-human identities is getting easier while finding a person willing to be accountable for one is harder. I agree. Shrinking an access window without a lifecycle underneath it just times out access that nobody remembers approving. Measure what moves. Share of identities with an accepted owner, count of high-scoring identities, age of the oldest unrotated secret, share using short-lived credentials, and time from discovery to closure.

Nobody wants the owner field. Being named owner feels like taking on risk. If the only consequence is a nagging email, people decline or click through. Make the route to ownership easy and the alternative clear, and expect the first sweep to be slow. Sources disagree. The same identity has a different name in the directory, the cloud and the vault. Merging them takes judgment, and a wrong merge hides a real finding. A big queue gets ignored. Thousands of tickets on day one teach everyone to stop looking. Release a working slice at a time. Federation moves the risk.

A loose trust condition can be worse than the key it replaced, since it is easy to miss. Review the rules as carefully as you reviewed the secrets. The score gets treated as truth. It orders the work and nothing more. A low score on an identity that is plainly exposed still gets fixed. Agents multiply faster than reviews. AI agents hold keys, tokens and delegated access like any other machine identity, and they appear faster than a quarterly review can follow. Treat them as part of this inventory from the start. See The AI Stack Nobody Approved .

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: I start with ownership and treat scoring as the second job. A perfect score on an ownerless list changes nothing. When I begin with the people who run the systems, the rest goes faster. I show the inventory to owners before I publish it. They find the mistakes in minutes, and they are more willing to accept an entry they have seen than one that appears in a report. I keep the formula small and write the arithmetic down. If a system owner can recompute their own score on paper, the argument moves from the number to the fix.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: I ask whether the secret is needed before I ask how to rotate it. The best answer is often to retire or replace, and asking first saves a lot of work. I treat the trust rules for federation as inventory too. They are small and easy to forget, and they decide who gets in. I close items on evidence. A re-scan result goes in the ticket. I would rather close fewer items and defend each one. I put expiry in at creation. Cleaning up later is always more expensive than asking for an end date on day one.

Most PAM programs stop once the passwords are in a vault. The risk that is left is access that never expires. Modernizing means four things working together: vault the secret, rotate it, put a recorded session in front of it, and grant access only for the length of the task. Every one of those steps has to leave evidence an auditor can check without asking you to explain it.

Privileged accounts are the ones that can change the system itself: domain admins, database owners, root on servers, cloud administrators, and service accounts with wide rights. Attackers want them because a valid account looks like normal activity. MITRE ATT&CK tracks this as Valid Accounts (T1078) . Standing privilege makes it worse. If an admin group has forty members, then forty people, and any malware running as them, can reach every system that group covers, at any hour, whether or not they are doing admin work. When an admin signs in interactively to a workstation, credential material can stay in that machine’s memory.
That is why credential dumping (T1003) is such a common step right after the first foothold.

The vault is there, but the old door is still open. Passwords are stored centrally, yet admins can still log in directly because nobody closed the direct path. Rotation skips the hard accounts. The accounts nobody dares touch are the ones hard-coded in scripts or shared between teams. Session recording is patchy. Some systems are covered and some are not, so a reviewer cannot answer “what did they actually do?” “Temporary” access is never taken back. Nobody owns the expiry.

A privileged session has to pass through a few controls, in order. If one is missing, the others can be walked around. The diagram shows the path a request takes, and where evidence is written along the way. A request passes five checkpoints in order. The audit store sits outside the systems being administered, so the people being recorded cannot change the record. Step 6 removes the access again. Products split this work differently, but the functions are the same.

In CyberArk’s self-hosted architecture, for example, the Vault stores the secrets, the Central Policy Manager (CPM) generates new passwords and replaces them on the target machines, and the Privileged Session Manager (PSM) records sessions and can restrict commands. Other platforms combine or separate these roles. What matters is that all of the functions exist and that none can be skipped. CyberArk architecture reference .

x: Ask for a specific thing The engineer names the target, the reason, a ticket or change number, and how long they need. “Admin on everything” is not a valid request. Guardrail Ticket must exist and be open Evidence Request record

Prove who they are Sign-in goes through single sign-on with multi-factor authentication. For the most sensitive systems, that means phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 keys, not SMS or push approvals. Guardrail No MFA, no request Evidence Sign-in log

Approve by policy, or by a person Low-risk, pre-agreed roles can be approved automatically. Access to production or to the identity systems themselves needs a named human, and for the most critical, two. Guardrail Requester cannot approve their own request Evidence Approver, time, reason

h: Approve by policy, or by a person
x: Connect through the broker The engineer opens a session through the PAM broker. The broker uses the credential on their behalf, so the person never sees or types the password. Guardrail Direct login to the target is blocked at the network Evidence Full session recording

Work, and be recorded Commands and screens are recorded. Where the platform supports it, dangerous commands can be blocked or flagged in real time. Guardrail Recording cannot be turned off by the user Evidence Searchable recording tied to the ticket

Access ends on its own When the time runs out or the session closes, access is removed and the secret is changed, so a copied password is worthless. Guardrail Expiry is enforced by the system, not by memory Evidence Rotation log

One shared database admin password, known to a whole team. Not changed for over a year, because changing it might break a script. The engineer logs in directly. Nothing records what they ran. After an incident, nobody can say who did what.

The engineer asks for two hours on that database, citing the incident ticket. The on-call manager approves from their phone. The session runs through the broker and is recorded. At the end, access closes and the credential is rotated. The recording is linked to the ticket.

Zero Standing Privilege means nobody holds admin rights by default. Access is created for a task and removed when it ends. This lines up with a tenet in NIST’s Zero Trust Architecture (SP 800-207): access to each resource is granted per session, with the least privilege needed to finish the task. Illustrative only. The point is the shape: with standing access the attack surface is the whole week. With just-in-time access it is only the short windows when someone had an approved reason to be there.

Friction breeds workarounds. If getting access takes an hour, people will keep a back-door account. Make the approved path the quickest one. The PAM platform becomes the target. Move people to phishing-resistant sign-in in risk order: privileged users first, then people who reach high-risk apps, then everyone else. One company-wide date puts the heaviest support load on the day you can least afford it. Recovery decides whether the program works. If a lost key can be fixed with a text message or a password reset, an attacker will use that route instead of the strong one. Keep a fallback during each wave and retire it only when adoption and help-desk data say the wave is stable. Legacy apps and break-glass accounts get named plans, not quiet exceptions.

Most workforces still sign in with a password and something extra: a text message code, an app code, or a push notification to approve. That is better than a password alone, and it is still phishable. A convincing fake sign-in page can collect the password and the code together and replay them to the real site. CISA’s phishing-resistant MFA fact sheet lists SMS and voice codes, push notifications without number matching and app one-time codes without number matching as forms of MFA that remain open to phishing, and it calls SMS and voice a last resort. Phishing-resistant sign-in closes that gap.

It also creates a project that is easy to get wrong. A blanket rollout can lock out the users least ready for it, while the accounts most worth protecting wait on the same generic timeline as everyone else. The administrator who can change every other account’s access ends up in the same queue as a part-time user of a low-risk tool. So I start with practical questions. Who needs it most? What happens the day someone loses the device? Which applications cannot take a modern sign-in at all?
And how will we know that people use the new method and do not drift back to the old one?

WebAuthn. The W3C Web Authentication standard. It defines an API for creating and using public key credentials that are scoped to the site that created them. A credential can only be used with the same relying party it was registered with, which is why a look-alike site gets nothing useful. Passkey. The FIDO Alliance describes a passkey as a FIDO authentication credential that lets a person sign in with the same process they use to unlock their device: a biometric, a PIN or a pattern. Device-bound and synced.

FIDO describes synced passkeys as credentials synced between a person’s devices through a cloud service, and device-bound passkeys as ones that never leave a single device, such as those on a security key. Attestation. Evidence about the make and model of an authenticator, which a relying party can ask for at registration. Authenticator assurance levels (AAL). NIST SP 800-63B uses these to describe how much confidence a sign-in gives. In the current revision, applications assessed at AAL2 have to offer a phishing-resistant option, and AAL3 requires a non-exportable private key and phishing resistance. Authentication strength.

Microsoft Entra’s name for a conditional access control that requires a set of methods. It has three built-in strengths: multifactor, passwordless and phishing-resistant. Phishing-resistant includes FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business or a platform credential, and certificate-based authentication. I use Microsoft Entra as the worked example because its documentation is public and I checked it for this page. The same slots exist in other identity providers.

Logging runs under all of it. The dots show a sign-in. The first dot follows the normal path: the device signs, the identity provider checks, the policy decides, and the resource gets a token. The identity provider checks the signature against the public key it holds for that user (2, with the policy engine asking who, what and how risky). h: How a passkey sign-in fits together
x: If the user has no usable key, the policy does not fall back to a weaker method. It sends them to recovery (4), and recovery ends with a new passkey (5). Break-glass accounts stay outside the policy so a bad rule cannot lock everyone out, and every use alerts a person (6). Two details from the Microsoft documentation shape the design. An authentication strength is evaluated after the initial sign-in, so it does not by itself limit which method a user starts with. And sign-in risk and user risk need Entra ID Protection.

x: The per-user score I describe below is a separate, advisory input for planning waves. It never blocks anyone on its own.

I run the move as waves. Each wave has a guardrail that has to hold and evidence that shows it held. Inventory methods and device posture Before setting an order, list which authentication methods each person has registered and what devices they sign in from. Readiness is uneven and assuming otherwise is how the least prepared users get locked out. In a directory such as Entra, the authentication methods activity report shows registration and usage by method, which gives a starting picture. Guardrail No wave is planned from assumptions Evidence Method and device inventory, agreed with the owners

Score and order the waves Add an advisory risk score per user and device. It draws on things like privilege, access to sensitive apps, current method strength and device condition, and it can be rules, a model, or both. The score proposes an order. A person owns the order. Highest-risk accounts go first. Guardrail The score advises and a named owner decides Evidence Wave list with the owner’s sign-off

The section on recovery below covers the design. Guardrail No enrollment until recovery is written and tested Evidence Recovery runbook and a test record

Registration is a sign-in that matters, so it needs a strong prior sign-in. Entra requires a user to have completed MFA within the past five minutes before registering a passkey (FIDO2). Guardrail Two authenticators per person before enforcement Evidence Registration report by user

Enforce by wave, report-only first Turn the phishing-resistant requirement on for one population at a time. Microsoft’s own guidance is to confirm a policy in report-only mode before switching it on. Exclude the break-glass group deliberately and document why. Guardrail Report-only results reviewed before enforcement Evidence Policy impact review and the exclusion record

Keep the fallback, and watch the data During each wave a fallback path stays available. I watch adoption, sign-in failures and help-desk tickets for that population. If tickets climb or people keep using the old method, the wave is not done, whatever the calendar says. Guardrail Fallback stays until the exit criteria are met Evidence Adoption and ticket data per wave

x: Retire the weak methods for that population Once adoption and ticket data confirm the wave is stable, remove passwords and weak methods for those users and take the fallback away. Then move to the next wave. This is how the highest-risk accounts end up on phishing-resistant sign-in ahead of the general population, and how help-desk load spreads across waves instead of landing on one cutover date. Guardrail Fallback removal needs a named approver Evidence Change record and a method report showing what is left

Privileged — Administrators and people who can change access for others — Device-bound authenticators, phishing-resistant strength required, no weak fallback 2. High-risk apps — Everyone who reaches finance, HR, source code, customer data or identity tools — Phishing-resistant strength required for those apps first, with a short fallback window 3.

A strong sign-in method is only as strong as the way back in. If a user who loses a key can reset it by answering a text message, the text message is now the real sign-in. NIST SP 800-63B-4 treats recovery as its own topic (Sec. 4.2), including saved recovery codes and a notification to the user after recovery (Sec. 4.2.3). I did not verify the full list of recovery methods and requirements, so read that section before you write yours. What I design for is a recovery that repairs the strong method and does not step around it.

Four cases come up again and again. Lost or broken device, second key available. The person signs in with the other authenticator and registers a replacement. This is the cheap case, and it is why I want two authenticators for everyone before enforcement. Lost device, no second key. The help desk verifies identity with a process that does not rely on anything the attacker could phish, such as a video call with the manager present, or in person. Then it issues a time-limited pass.

In Entra, a Temporary Access Pass is a time-limited passcode, configured for one use or several, that lets a user onboard passwordless methods and makes recovery easier when a strong method is lost. Its lifetime is configurable, with a default of one hour, and a single-use pass needs the registration finished within 10 minutes of sign-in. The user registers a new passkey straight away. New joiner. The same pass, issued at day one after HR and the manager confirm the person, ideally handed over alongside a security key. The first thing a new joiner does is register two authenticators. Privileged user.

I raise the bar: in person or two-person approval, a shorter pass, and an alert to the security team. A recovery for an administrator is a high-risk event and gets treated as one. The Entra documentation notes that a Temporary Access Pass cannot be used with the Network Policy Server extension or the AD FS adapter, so check where else a pass will not work. Whatever the product, the pass is itself a credential. It is short-lived, issued by a verified process, sent to a verified channel, and logged, and the user is told when it is issued.

h: Device-bound or synced, and what attestation changes
x: The choice between device-bound and synced passkeys is a risk decision. NIST SP 800-63B-4 says syncable authenticators cannot be used at AAL3 because the private key has to be exportable, and it allows them at AAL2 and below. That gives a simple starting rule: device-bound for people and apps that need the top level of assurance, and synced passkeys where AAL2 is the target and the convenience is worth it. Microsoft’s passkey documentation adds three practical points. When attestation is enforced at registration, Entra can verify the make and model of the authenticator against trusted metadata.

h: Device-bound or synced, and what attestation changes
x: When it is not enforced, Entra cannot guarantee any attribute of a passkey, including whether it is synced or device-bound. And the documentation advises treating synced passkeys as phishing-resistant credentials with the same security posture as other unattested authenticators. Its synced passkey page adds that synced passkeys do not support attestation, and suggests device-bound passkeys such as security keys or passkeys in Microsoft Authenticator for admins and highly privileged users. So the policy I write has two profiles. Privileged users and the highest-risk apps require attested, device-bound authenticators. Everyone else may use synced passkeys.

h: Device-bound or synced, and what attestation changes
x: Entra supports this with passkey profiles, which are named sets of rules that govern registration and sign-in for targeted groups, and it allows up to three of them, including the default. Two cautions from the same page. Key restrictions, which allow or block authenticators by AAGUID, apply to both registration and sign-in, so removing an allowed AAGUID stops people who registered that model from signing in. And attestation is checked only at registration, so users who registered without it are not blocked later if you turn it on.

h: Legacy apps that cannot do modern sign-in
x: Every program meets the application that only knows a username and password. I handle these in the open. List them, give each an owner, and pick one of four routes. Put it behind the identity provider. If the app can speak SAML or OpenID Connect, move it to single sign-on so the policy applies. OMB M-22-09 asks that MFA be enforced at the application layer, not only at the network layer. Upgrade or replace it.

h: Legacy apps that cannot do modern sign-in
x: CISA’s fact sheet advises a plan to either upgrade systems that do not support MFA or migrate away from them, and to escalate the risk of any system that does not support MFA to senior leadership. I follow that literally. The owner of the risk gets the decision in writing. Contain it. Where neither is possible yet, narrow who can reach it, put it on a restricted network path, scope its accounts and monitor its sign-ins more closely. Block legacy protocols where you can.

h: Legacy apps that cannot do modern sign-in
x: In Entra, legacy authentication clients, such as POP3, IMAP4 and SMTP, do not support MFA or pass device state, so conditional access grant controls like requiring MFA or a compliant device block them. Check what depends on them first. Anything left over goes on the exception register with an owner, a reason, a compensating control and an end date, reviewed on a rhythm. An exception with no end date is a decision nobody made.

Emergency access accounts are the part of a passwordless program that people forget until a policy locks them out. Microsoft recommends two or more emergency access accounts, authenticated with a passkey (FIDO2) or certificate-based authentication, using phishing-resistant methods that differ from those of the normal admin accounts. It also recommends excluding a dedicated group from conditional access policies that block or restrict sign-in, monitoring their sign-in and audit logs with alerts, and testing them at regular intervals, at least every 90 days. The interaction I plan for is simple.

Each new wave and each new policy gets a check that the emergency accounts still work and still alert. Break-glass accounts belong in the first wave, because they are privileged by definition. The full design is in Break-Glass Access .

The help desk is where recovery meets people, so it needs its own script. The agent proves identity with the agreed method, issues a time-limited pass, and never reads out or resets a password as a shortcut. The ticket records who verified whom, how, and when the pass was issued. A recovery for a privileged account goes to a second person. After recovery the user gets a notice on a channel the requester does not control, and the old authenticators are reviewed and removed if they are lost.
This is an illustration of the flow, not a specific event or company.

Signs in with a password and approves a push notification on a phone. Has one registered method, so a lost phone means a help-desk call. Recovery over the phone with a few personal questions. Sits in the same wave as every other user.

Signs in with a security key and a PIN. Phishing-resistant strength is required for admin roles. Has a second key stored securely, so a lost key is a swap. If both are lost: video call with the manager, then a short-lived pass issued by a second person, then a new key at once. The recovery alerts the security team and notifies the admin. The fallback stayed in place for this group for the first weeks and was removed only after adoption and ticket data looked stable. The general population follows the same flow in a later wave, with synced passkeys on managed devices.

Done when The inventory is agreed with its owners and recovery is written down. 2. Pilot Run the identity team and a few volunteers through enrollment, sign-in, loss and recovery. Done when Every recovery case has been tried at least once and the runbook has been corrected. 3. Done when Admin roles cannot sign in with a weak method and the emergency accounts have been tested. 4.

Recovery becomes the weak door. Teams harden sign-in and leave password reset or phone verification in place. Attackers go to whichever door is easier. Enforcing too early. A strict policy that was never run in report-only mode catches the shared mailbox, the service desk tool or the executive assistant’s old laptop. Treating synced and device-bound as the same. Without attestation you cannot tell them apart, so the policy cannot treat them differently. The fallback never goes away. If weak methods stay registered, an attacker can ask for them. Users, too, will drift back to the familiar one. Legacy apps on an endless exception.
Without owners and end dates, the long tail stays long.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: These are habits I keep, not a checklist from any one project. Start from the data, then talk to the owners. I inventory methods and devices first, and then walk the list with the people who own each group. The order comes from that conversation, with the score as an input. Write recovery first. I used to treat it as a support detail for later. Now I write it before the first enrollment, and I try to break it in the pilot. Ask for two authenticators from day one. It is easier to ask at enrollment than to chase people after the first loss.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: Make the fallback expire. Every fallback gets a review date and a named approver when I create it. Treat the help desk as part of the design. I sit in on calls, read the tickets and change the script, because the control lives there as much as in the policy. Test the emergency accounts every wave. I do it even when the last test passed. A new policy is a new chance to lock them out. The broader approach, from first conversation to last training session, is in How I Run a Privileged Access Program .

Feature lists do not settle a platform decision. A scenario that one tool handles and another only half handles does. I write the scenarios, weights and pass marks first, run every candidate through the same scripts, and score before anyone argues. The result is a decision record that links what the tool can do to integration, operations, audit and who will own it.

The markets for privileged access, non-human identity (NHI) and cloud security move fast. Tools overlap, names change and every demo looks good. A feature checklist rewards the vendor with the longest list, not the one that fits the organization. The harder part is that the people in the room want different things. Security wants control, engineers want speed, audit wants evidence and finance wants a number. A decision made from demos alone tends to favor whoever presented last. I want a method that survives those disagreements and can be explained a year later.

It starts with people, not products. I talk to stakeholders in different business units to understand their risks, how security affects their users, what compliance and audit need from them, what infrastructure they run, which regions they work in and how the organization is structured. That becomes a written pain list. Then I recommend proofs of concept with different tools, look at the results and decide which to buy. Once licenses and tools are procured, professional services take over the build. The dot follows one evaluation from the first conversation to the handover.
The bar under the middle stages is the point of the method: the rules are written before the first demo and they do not change per vendor.

Scenario-led assessments built around identity types, trust boundaries and lifecycle responsibilities. Proof-of-concept work on Delinea Secret Server and Privileged Remote Access, focused on practical use cases. Product analysis and operating-model planning for StrongDM, alongside structured assessments of Clutch Security and Wiz. This page is about the method. It does not compare or rank those products, and nothing here is a statement about what any of them can or cannot do. For that, read the vendor’s own documentation and run your own scenarios.

I build the catalog around identity types, because each one has a different trust boundary and a different lifecycle owner. Each row becomes a test script. The scenarios are examples of the shape, not a complete list.

Identity type — Example scenario — What the script checks Human privileged — An on-call engineer needs admin access to a production server at night — Request and approval, session start, recording, and what happens when the approval expires mid-session Service account — A database service account password is rotated while the application is running — Rotation without an outage, the owner recorded, and a clear alert if rotation fails API key or token — A third-party integration token nears expiry — Discovery of the token, an owner attached, rotation or revocation, and a read log SSH key — A shared deployment key sits on many servers — Finding where it is, replacing it with per-user or short-lived access, removing the old key Cloud workload — A container needs a database login at start-up — Fetching a short-lived credential at runtime with no secret baked into the image CI/CD pipeline — A deployment job needs a cloud credential — Scoped access for one job, no long-lived secret in pipeline variables, a trace of which run used it AI agent — An agent calls an internal API on a user’s behalf — Whose identity it acts under, how narrow the access is, how it is stopped, and whether its actions are logged

Scenario results are one input. I group the rest into nine criteria and agree the weights with the sponsor before the first demo. A few items are gates that a tool must pass regardless of its score, such as a data-residency requirement. Gates are pass or fail and sit outside the weighting.

Criterion — What I ask — Example evidence Security controls — Does it enforce least privilege, approval, session control and secret protection in our scenarios? — POC script results Coverage — How many of our scenarios does it handle directly, and how many need a workaround? — Scenario catalog, marked per tool Integration — Does it work with our service desk, directory and SIEM without custom glue? — Integration test with ServiceNow, Entra and the SIEM High availability and DR — What happens to access when it is down, and how fast can it be restored? — Outage test and recovery notes Deployment model — Does SaaS, self-hosted or hybrid fit our regions and data rules? — Architecture review Operating model and skills — Who runs it, what skills do they need, and how much daily effort does it take? — Run-book draft and effort estimate Audit evidence — Can I answer who, what, when and approved by whom, from the tool itself? — Sample reports and log export Licensing and total cost — How is it priced, and what does it cost once services, training and support are in? — Quote with assumptions written down Vendor viability, roadmap and support — Will the vendor and the product be here in five years, and how do they handle problems? — Due-diligence pack, references, support terms

Listen and write the pain list Interviews across the business units, then a one-page list of the risks, user frictions, audit needs and regional or infrastructure limits. The sponsor signs it off. Guardrail Pain list agreed before tools are named Evidence Interview notes, signed list

h: Listen and write the pain list
x: Write scenarios, weights and gates Pick the scenarios from the catalog that match the pain list, set the weights and the gates, and write pass marks for each script step. Guardrail Criteria dated before the first demo Evidence Criteria document

Design the proof of concept Success criteria in writing before starting. A fixed time box, a test environment with no real secrets, a named person who runs each test, and the same scripts for every tool. The scripts include failure cases: the vault is down, a rotation fails, an access grant is revoked mid-session. Guardrail Same scripts, same time box, test data only Evidence POC plan, environment review

Run it and log everything Each tool is set up and tested by the same people where possible. Every bit of vendor help is logged, because help during a trial may not exist in production. Guardrail Vendor assistance recorded Evidence Run log, support log

Score on your own first Each scorer fills in a sheet alone, then we compare. Where scores differ by two points or more, we go back to the evidence and not to opinion. Guardrail Independent scoring before discussion Evidence Individual score sheets

Check the vendor Due diligence runs alongside the trial, covered in the next section. A strong trial does not cancel a weak answer here. Guardrail Security review before production access Evidence Due-diligence pack

Write the decision record What was chosen and why, the scores, the trade-offs, the risks accepted and who accepted them, and any dissent. Guardrail Risk acceptance named Evidence Signed decision record

Hand over Once licenses are bought, the statement of work, the engagement letter, the training program and support terms go to professional services. The scenarios and scripts become acceptance tests for the build, and the POC findings feed the architecture. Guardrail POC scripts reused as acceptance tests Evidence SOW, training plan, architecture inputs

Success criteria first. For each script, write what a pass, a partial and a fail look like before anyone touches a tool. One script, every tool. If a script has to change for one tool, it changes for all of them and the earlier runs are repeated. A fixed time box. Two weeks per tool is an example. The number matters less than giving every candidate the same. A test environment that looks like ours. Same network zones, same directory integration and similar target systems, with test credentials only. A named runner. Someone from our side runs the tests.

Vendor staff can advise, and that is logged. Failure cases on purpose. Take the vault offline, break a rotation, revoke access while a session is open, lose the connection to the directory. The way a tool fails says more than the way it works.
Everything in this section is illustrative. The candidates are labeled A, B and C, are not real products, and the results are invented to show the method.

h: One scenario: rotate a service account password
x: Script step — Candidate A — Candidate B — Candidate C Rotate the password on a schedule — Pass — Pass — Pass Application picks up the new value — Pass — Partial, needed a restart — Pass Force a failure halfway through rotation — Alert raised, old value kept — No alert, left inconsistent — Alert raised, needed a manual fix Read log shows who fetched it — Pass — Pass — Pass Score for this scenario (0 to 3) — 3 — 1 — 2 Candidate B’s happy path was fine.

h: One scenario: rotate a service account password
x: The failure step is where the scores separated, which is why failure cases are in every script. A scenario score of 3 means the pass mark was met with no workaround, 2 needed a manual step, 1 needed significant effort, 0 could not be done.

h: Adding it up, and testing the weights
x: Weighted points are the weight times the 0 to 3 score, summed. Four criteria are shown for brevity. Criterion (excerpt) — Weight — A — B — C Security controls — 20 — 3 — 2 — 2 Integration — 12 — 2 — 3 — 1 High availability and DR — 10 — 1 — 2 — 3 Audit evidence — 10 — 2 — 2 — 2 Weighted points (max 156) — 114 — 116 — 102 Same, after moving 5 weight points from integration to HA and DR — 109 — 111 — 112 Two things to notice.

h: Adding it up, and testing the weights
x: The totals are close, so the total alone cannot decide anything. And a small change to the weights reorders the candidates. Whenever the order moves that easily, I do not treat the number as the answer. I go back to the scenarios and the gates, and I ask the sponsor which weights they really believe.

Write first. Criteria and weights come before the demos, so they cannot be shaped around a favorite. Score alone, then talk. Early opinions anchor the room. Rotate the order. Do not always run the same tool first or last, and note who presented when. Treat vendor effort as data. If a vendor engineer configured something for us, the operating-model score reflects that we could not have done it ourselves on day one. Test the weights. Move them around as above, and see whether the decision survives. Bring in someone who did not attend.
A reader from audit or security architecture who reads only the record, and asks what is missing.

h: Security due diligence on the vendor
x: The product may be good and still be a poor thing to trust with your most privileged credentials. I ask for, and read, the following before any production access is granted: Certifications and audit reports. Which reports, what scope, what dates, and whether the product I am buying sits inside that scope. Penetration-test summaries. Recent, independent, with findings and how they were closed. Data residency. Where data and backups live, where support staff can access it from, and which sub-processors are involved. Vulnerability handling. How issues are reported, how fast patches arrive and how customers are told. Exit and data export.

h: Security due diligence on the vendor
x: How I get my secrets, policies and audit logs out in a usable form, and what happens to my data when the contract ends. Viability and support. Support hours and escalation, references I can call, and what the roadmap commits to in writing. Open questions are written into the decision record. An unanswered question is a risk that someone has to accept by name.

Business sponsor — The problem statement, the budget and the final decision Product owner (me, in this role) — The evaluation plan, the scenario catalog, the scoring method and the decision record Security architecture — Security criteria, the vendor due-diligence review and the risk acceptance Platform and infrastructure teams — Test environments, integration tests and the operating-model estimate Procurement and legal — Commercial terms, contract language and exit clauses Internal audit — Independent view of whether the process was followed The decision belongs to the business. I prepare the analysis and the recommendation. The sponsor decides. Someone owns the product afterwards.
The evaluation names the product owner and the platform team before contracts are signed, so ownership does not become a question after go-live.

The decision is already made. If a tool was chosen informally, the POC becomes theatre. It is better to say so and adjust the scope. Demos replace tests. A polished demo shows a scripted path. Only your own scripts show yours. The POC is too easy. A clean test network hides directory quirks, proxy rules and legacy systems that decide the real effort. The happy path wins. Without failure cases, a tool that fails badly can still score well. Total cost is missed. Licenses are one line. Services, training, infrastructure, support and the people to run it add up. Scope drifts to a bigger product.

Cloud security, NHI and PAM overlap. Decide which problem you are solving, or the comparison stops being fair. Handover is forgotten. The POC learning sits in one person’s head and professional services start from nothing.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: These are habits I keep, not a record of any one project. I write the pass marks before I see the tool. It is much harder to be fair afterwards. I test how things fail. I put the outage and the failed rotation in every script. I keep vendor help in a log. It shows the real effort of running the tool later. I treat the score as a prompt for questions. When totals are close I go back to the scenarios and the evidence. I write the exit plan during the evaluation.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: It is easier to ask about data export before a contract than after. I involve the operators early. The people who will run the platform estimate the effort, not the people who will only buy it. I hand over the scripts. Reused as acceptance tests, they tie the purchase to what we were promised.
